title: Cloth: how thread is woven, knitted and stitched, and how old cloth is used again

summary.text: Pull a T-shirt sideways and it stretches. Pull a handkerchief and it hardly moves, though both may be cotton. The difference is in how the thread is arranged: a handkerchief is woven from crossing threads, and a T-shirt is knitted from one thread in loops. Your child measures that stretch, finds where it comes from, and tests how small a stitch must be to hold mustard seeds. They also meet the baya weaver and the tailorbird, the silk moth, and the weavers, dyers and embroiderers of many parts of India. Last, they find out how old cloth is mended, remade and recycled.
summary.art: A child stretching a red T-shirt sideways with both hands, beside a checked cotton handkerchief pulled tight and flat, with a small drawing of looped thread over the T-shirt and crossed threads over the handkerchief.

intro.hook: Take a cotton T-shirt and a cotton handkerchief. Pull each one sideways. The T-shirt stretches a lot, and the handkerchief hardly at all. Both are made of cotton thread. So why does only one of them stretch?
intro.text: The answer is not in the cotton. It is in the path the thread takes. In the handkerchief, hundreds of threads cross each other, over and under. This is weaving. In the T-shirt, one long thread is pulled into row after row of loops. This is knitting. Humans are not the only animals who do this kind of work. A male baya weaver knots and weaves a hanging nest from strips of grass, using only his beak and feet. A tailorbird stitches a leaf into a cup with plant fibre. In this unit you take cloth apart to see how it is made, and you make and test some yourself.
intro.art: A phone camera held close over a handkerchief showing criss-cross threads on its screen, and beside it a T-shirt whose close-up shows rows of small loops.

outcomes: By the end I can explain weaving with the words warp and weft, and tell a woven cloth from a knitted one by looking and by pulling.
By the end I can explain why knitted cloth stretches more than woven cloth, using the thread lengths I measured in Woven or Knitted.
By the end I can say how fibres are spun into yarn, and sort fibres into plant, animal and synthetic, with one good point and one cost of each.
By the end I can tell the life of the silk moth in order, and give two sides of the argument about silk.
By the end I can sew a running stitch and a backstitch, and explain how stitch length changes a seam, using my Leaky Seam results.
By the end I can explain why a cut edge frays and how a hem or a selvedge stops it.
By the end I can name cloth traditions from at least four parts of India, and say whether each pattern is woven, dyed, printed or stitched.
By the end I can say how a baya weaver and a tailorbird build, and give four ways to use old cloth again before it becomes waste.

terms.meaning: A very thin strand, like a hair. Cloth begins as fibres from a plant, an animal or a factory.
terms.example: Pull a lamp wick apart and you find cotton fibres, each about 2 or 3 centimetres long.
terms.art: A fluffy cotton wick pulled open, with one single fibre held between two fingers.

terms.meaning: A long thread made by twisting many fibres together. Sewing thread, knitting wool and the threads in cloth are all yarns.
terms.example: One yarn pulled out of a towel is many times longer than any fibre in it.
terms.art: A ball of wool with its loose end untwisting into fine fibres.

terms.meaning: Drawing fibres out and twisting them into yarn. The twist presses the fibres together, and friction stops them sliding apart.
terms.example: A charkha is a spinning wheel. Its spindle turns fast and twists cotton into yarn.
terms.art: A woman at a box charkha, a line of thread running from her raised hand to the spinning spindle.

terms.meaning: One of the thinner yarns that are twisted together to make a thicker, steadier yarn.
terms.example: Untwist a piece of sewing thread and it opens into 2 or 3 plies.
terms.art: A thick thread untwisted at the end into three thinner strands.

terms.meaning: A staple fibre is short, like cotton or wool, and must be spun. A filament is one very long fibre, like silk or nylon.
terms.example: One cotton fibre is about 3 centimetres long. The filament from one silk cocoon can be many hundreds of metres long.
terms.art: A short curly cotton fibre beside a long smooth thread that runs off the edge of the picture.

terms.meaning: Making cloth by crossing two sets of threads, over and under each other, at right angles.
terms.example: A handkerchief, a bedsheet, a sari and a gunny sack are all woven.
terms.art: A close-up of plain cloth showing threads crossing over and under like a tiny mat.

terms.meaning: The threads that run along the length of a woven cloth. On the loom they are stretched tight before weaving starts.
terms.example: On the Chindi Coaster loom, the string wound up and down the card is the warp.
terms.art: A cardboard loom with strings running from top to bottom, labelled 'warp'.

terms.meaning: The thread that runs across a woven cloth. The weaver passes it over and under the warp threads, row after row.
terms.example: On the Chindi Coaster loom, the cloth strips you weave from side to side are the weft.
terms.art: A strip of cloth being passed over and under the strings of a cardboard loom, labelled 'weft'.

terms.meaning: A frame or machine that holds the warp threads tight, so that the weft can be woven through them.
terms.example: A handloom is worked by a person's hands and feet. A power loom is driven by an electric motor.
terms.art: A woman sitting at a wooden pit loom, her feet on pedals below floor level and a shuttle in her hand.

terms.meaning: The firm side edge of a woven cloth, where the weft thread turns back. It has no cut ends, so it does not fray.
terms.example: The long edges of a sari, a dupatta or a thorthu towel are selvedges.
terms.art: The edge of a towel in close-up, showing the cross thread turning back in small U-turns.

terms.meaning: Making cloth from one long yarn by pulling it into rows of loops. Each loop hangs from another loop.
terms.example: T-shirts, banians, socks and sweaters are knitted.
terms.art: A close-up of sweater stitches, one thread coloured red to show its looping path across a row.

terms.meaning: To come apart at a cut edge, as loose threads slide out of a woven cloth.
terms.example: The cut edge of a torn dupatta soon grows a fringe of loose threads.
terms.art: A square of cloth with one edge turned into a fringe of loose threads.

terms.meaning: A line of stitches that joins two pieces of cloth.
terms.example: Turn a shirt inside out and you can see the seams along the sides and around the sleeves.
terms.art: A shirt turned inside out, with arrows pointing to the stitched lines at the side and shoulder.

terms.meaning: An edge of cloth folded over and stitched down. It hides the cut ends, so the edge does not fray.
terms.example: The bottom edge of a school skirt, a kurta or a curtain is hemmed.
terms.art: The lower edge of a kurta folded up to show the fold and its line of stitches.

terms.meaning: The simplest stitch. The needle goes up and down through the cloth along a line, leaving a dashed line of thread.
terms.example: Kantha quilts are covered with rows of running stitch through layers of old cloth.
terms.art: A dashed line of thread on a cloth, with a needle halfway through the next stitch.

terms.meaning: A stitch in which each new stitch goes back to meet the end of the last one, so the thread makes one unbroken line.
terms.example: A backstitch seam is stronger than a running stitch seam, and uses about three times as much thread.
terms.art: A solid line of stitches on cloth, with small arrows showing the needle going back, then forward.

terms.meaning: A fibre made by a living being. Cotton, jute, coir and linen come from plants. Wool and silk come from animals.
terms.example: A cotton kurta, a jute bag, a coir doormat and a woollen shawl are made of natural fibres.
terms.art: A cotton boll, a jute stem, a coconut husk, a sheep and a silk cocoon in one row.

terms.meaning: A fibre made in a factory from chemicals, mostly from petroleum. Nylon, polyester and acrylic are synthetic fibres.
terms.example: Most school bags, raincoats and sports jerseys are made of polyester or nylon.
terms.art: A machine head with many tiny holes, each pushing out a fine shiny thread.

terms.meaning: A yarn or cloth made of two or more kinds of fibre mixed together.
terms.example: A school shirt whose label says '65% polyester, 35% cotton' is a blend.
terms.art: A clothes label reading '65% polyester 35% cotton' sewn inside a collar.

terms.meaning: The case that a caterpillar spins around their own body before changing into a moth. A silk moth's cocoon is one long silk filament.
terms.example: A mulberry silk cocoon is about the size of a groundnut shell.
terms.art: A pale yellow oval cocoon on a twig, with a groundnut beside it for size.

terms.meaning: Cloth that is spun by hand and woven by hand.
terms.example: During the freedom struggle, Gandhi asked people to spin on the charkha and wear khadi.
terms.art: A folded stack of rough white handspun cloth beside a small charkha.

terms.meaning: A way of making a pattern by tying and dyeing the threads before they are woven. The pattern has soft, feathered edges.
terms.example: Pochampally in Telangana, Patan in Gujarat and Sambalpur in Odisha are known for ikat.
terms.art: A sari border with diamond shapes whose edges look slightly blurred, like a picture seen through moving water.

terms.meaning: Decorating cloth with stitches of thread after the cloth has been woven.
terms.example: Toda women of the Nilgiris embroider red and black patterns on cream cotton shawls.
terms.art: A needle pulling red thread through cream cloth to finish a small diamond pattern.

terms.meaning: A tiny piece of fibre, too small to see easily, that breaks off cloth when it is worn and washed.
terms.example: Scientists have found microfibres of polyester in beach sand on six continents.
terms.art: A greatly enlarged drop of wash water with a few short coloured threads floating in it.

explanations.concept: From fibre to yarn: spinning and plies
explanations.definition: A fibre is a very thin strand. Spinning draws fibres out and twists them together into a long yarn.
explanations.description: A cotton fibre is only about 2 or 3 centimetres long. A yarn can be kilometres long, because the fibres overlap and the twist presses them together. Friction between the pressed fibres stops them sliding apart. Short fibres such as cotton, wool and jute are called staple fibres, and they must be spun. Silk, nylon and polyester come as filaments, which are single fibres of great length, and they need only a light twist. A single spun yarn tends to untwist and curl. So two or three single yarns are twisted together in the opposite direction. Each one is called a ply. The plies try to untwist one way and the whole yarn tries to untwist the other way, so the yarn stays still. A takli is a small hand spindle. A charkha turns the spindle with a wheel, so one hand turns and the other draws out the cotton. A spinning mill does the same job on thousands of spindles at once.
examples: In Take a Thread Apart, a piece of thread opens into 2 or 3 plies, and each ply opens into short fibres.
A cotton lamp wick is fibres with very little twist, so it pulls apart easily. Kite string is tightly twisted, so it does not.
A coir rope from Kerala is made of two or three twisted strands of coconut fibre, twisted together the other way.
explanations.art: Three pictures in a row: loose cotton fibres, the same fibres twisted into one yarn, and three yarns twisted together into a thicker thread.

explanations.concept: Weaving: warp, weft and the loom
explanations.definition: Weaving makes cloth by crossing two sets of threads at right angles. The warp threads run along the length of the cloth. The weft thread runs across, over and under the warp.
explanations.description: A loom does four jobs. It holds the warp threads tight. It lifts some of them, so a gap opens between the lifted threads and the rest. A shuttle carries the weft thread through that gap. Then a comb-like bar pushes the new weft thread tight against the cloth. In plain weave the weft goes over one warp thread and under the next. It has the most crossings, so it is firm. In twill the weft goes over two or three threads and under one, and each row steps one thread sideways. That makes slanting lines, as in denim. In satin weave a thread floats over many threads before going under one, so the cloth is smooth and shiny but catches easily. Nothing in woven cloth is glued or knotted. Each thread is bent over and under the others, and friction at every crossing holds it in place. At the side edges the weft turns back, so the cloth has a firm edge called the selvedge.
examples: In Thread Paths, the handkerchief on the phone screen shows threads crossing like a tiny mat.
Jeans are blue outside and pale inside. In denim, the blue warp threads pass over three white weft threads and under one.
A gunny sack is plain weave in thick jute yarn, so the over and under pattern is easy to see without a lens.
A Pattamadai mat from Tirunelveli is woven the same way, with fine korai grass as the weft and cotton as the warp.
explanations.art: A simple loom seen from the side: tight warp threads, half of them lifted, a shuttle passing through the gap, and finished cloth rolled at the front.

explanations.definition: Knitting makes cloth from one long yarn pulled into rows of loops. Each loop passes through a loop in the row before it.
explanations.description: T-shirts, banians, socks, leggings and sweaters are knitted. Because the yarn runs in loops, a row of knitting uses much more yarn than the cloth is wide, often 3 or 4 times as much. When you pull knitted cloth, the loops change shape and the cloth grows longer. When you let go, the loops spring back. A woven thread is already nearly straight, so woven cloth has almost no length to spare. Knitted cloth stretches more across its rows than along its length. The stretch has a cost. If one loop breaks, the loops in its column can slip out one after another. This line of undone loops is called a ladder. The same fact has a use. A knitted sweater can be pulled back into one long yarn and knitted again. Most T-shirt cloth is knitted as a tube on round machines with hundreds of needles. Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu makes a large share of India's knitted clothes. Knitting is much younger than weaving. The oldest known knitted socks, from Egypt, are about 1,000 years old.
examples: In Woven or Knitted, the knitted strip stretches many times more than the woven strip under the same bottle.
In the same test, one row of thread pulled out of the knitted piece is far longer than the piece is wide.
A ladder in a sock or a pair of tights starts from a single broken loop.
Many families unravel an outgrown sweater, steam the crinkled wool straight and knit a new one.
explanations.art: A close-up drawing of knitted cloth with one row's thread coloured red, looping up and down across the picture, and below it the same red thread pulled out straight and much longer.

explanations.concept: Why a cut edge frays, and what stops it
explanations.definition: Fraying is the loss of threads from a cut edge of woven cloth. A thread near the edge slides out because nothing beyond it holds it in.
explanations.description: Inside a woven cloth, every thread is held by the threads that cross it. At a straight cut edge, the last thread that runs along the edge has crossing threads on one side only. Rubbing and washing push it off the ends of those threads, and then the next thread is the last one. The edge becomes a fringe. Three things slow this down. A selvedge has no cut ends, because the weft turns back at the edge. A hem folds the cut edge inside and stitches it down. A cut on the slant leaves no thread running along the edge, so no whole thread can slide off. Tailors also cut edges in zigzags with special scissors, so only short pieces can come away. Knitted cloth does not fray in this way. Its cut edge curls, and its loops can run into a ladder.
examples: In the Fray Test, the straight cut edge grows the widest fringe, and the selvedge grows none.
The fringe at the end of a towel or a dupatta is fraying done on purpose, then knotted so that it stops.
The inside seams of a ready-made shirt are wrapped in loops of thread by a machine, to stop the cut edges fraying.
explanations.art: Four cloth edges side by side: a straight cut with a long fringe, a zigzag cut with a short fringe, a slant cut with almost none, and a neat selvedge.

explanations.definition: A stitch is one pass of thread through cloth. A seam is a line of stitches that joins two pieces.
explanations.description: In a running stitch the needle goes down and up along a line. The thread lies on the top for one stitch and underneath for the next. It is quick, and it lets the cloth gather and ripple. But the two layers are pinned together only at the needle holes, so they can open between the holes. The longer the stitch, the wider the gap. In a backstitch the needle goes back to the end of the last stitch each time. The thread makes an unbroken line on top and a double line underneath. It holds better, takes longer and uses about three times as much thread. A sewing machine makes a lockstitch. One thread comes down with the needle, a second thread comes from a small spool underneath, and the two lock together inside the cloth at every stitch. A machine can make more than a thousand such stitches in a minute, each only 2 or 3 millimetres long. Tailoring is choosing: small stitches where a seam must hold, long stitches where it must be quick or must come out again.
examples: In the Leaky Seam Test, the seam with the longest stitches lets the most mustard seeds through.
A tailor tacks a blouse together with long running stitches for a fitting, then pulls them out after machine stitching.
A kantha quilt is held together by thousands of small running stitches through three or more layers of old cloth.
explanations.art: Three seams drawn from the side, cut through the cloth: a running stitch dipping in and out, a backstitch overlapping underneath, and a machine lockstitch with two threads hooked together inside the cloth.

explanations.concept: Natural fibres from plants and animals
explanations.definition: Natural fibres are made by living beings. Plant fibres are made mostly of cellulose. Animal fibres are made of protein.
explanations.description: Cotton fibres are hairs that grow on the seeds of the cotton plant. Each fibre is a single long cell. Cotton takes in water easily, so cotton clothes soak up sweat and feel cool, but they dry slowly and crease. Jute fibres come from the stem of the jute plant. Farmers in West Bengal, Assam and Bihar soak the cut stems in water for two or three weeks, until the fibres come loose. Jute is strong and rough, and India grows more of it than any other country. Coir comes from the husk of the coconut and stands up well to water. Linen comes from the stem of the flax plant. Wool is the hair of sheep. Each wool fibre is wavy and covered in tiny scales, so wool cloth traps a great deal of still air and keeps a body warm. Shepherd families of the Deccan weave coarse black wool into blankets called kambli. Pashmina is the fine under-hair of the Changthangi goat, who lives above 4,000 metres in Ladakh. Herders comb it out in spring, when the goats shed their winter coat.
examples: A thorthu towel from Kerala is thin cotton. It soaks up water fast and dries fast on a line.
Gunny sacks for rice and potatoes are jute, because jute is strong and cheap and lets air through.
A coir doormat stays outside in the monsoon for years without rotting.
A woollen sweater squeezed in the fist shrinks to a small lump, because most of the sweater is air.
explanations.art: A map of India with small pictures: a cotton boll on the Deccan, jute stems soaking in a pond in Bengal, coconut husks in Kerala, sheep on the Deccan plateau and a goat high in Ladakh.

explanations.concept: Silk and the life of the silk moth
explanations.definition: Silk is a filament spun by a caterpillar to make a cocoon. The mulberry silk moth has four stages of life: egg, caterpillar, pupa and moth.
explanations.description: A female silk moth lays several hundred eggs. Each egg hatches into a tiny caterpillar, often called a silkworm. The caterpillars eat only mulberry leaves. In about four weeks they shed their skin four times and grow to thousands of times their first weight. Then each caterpillar spins a cocoon around their own body, moving their head in a figure of eight for two or three days. The cocoon is one unbroken filament, many hundreds of metres long. Inside, the caterpillar becomes a pupa, and in about two weeks the pupa becomes a moth. The moth wets one end of the cocoon with a liquid that loosens the silk, and pushes out. That breaks the filament into many short pieces. So in most silk making, the cocoons are heated before the moths come out. The pupa inside dies, and the filament can be unwound whole. India makes four kinds of silk. Mulberry silk comes mostly from Karnataka. Tasar comes from wild moths in the forests of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. Golden muga silk comes only from Assam. Eri silk comes from Assam and Meghalaya.
examples: Ramanagara in Karnataka has one of the largest silk cocoon markets in Asia.
Eri cocoons are open at one end, and the moths usually leave before the silk is used. The silk is spun like cotton and is less shiny.
The mulberry silk moth has lived with people for about 5,000 years. The adult moths can no longer fly.

perspectives.explanation: Unbroken filament makes the strongest, shiniest silk. Many families earn their living from it, and the cooked pupae are used as feed and as food.

perspectives.who: Kusuma Rajaiah, a handloom technical officer from Hyderabad
perspectives.explanation: Around the year 2000 he worked out a way to let the moths come out first and then spin the broken cocoons. He called the cloth ahimsa silk.
The moths who come out cannot fly or feed and live only a few days. The silk costs more and is less shiny. So the gain for the moths is small.

explanations.art: A circle of four pictures joined by arrows: tiny eggs on paper, a pale caterpillar on a mulberry leaf, a cocoon cut open to show the brown pupa, and a cream moth beside an empty cocoon.

explanations.concept: Synthetic fibres, blends, and what all fibres share
explanations.definition: A synthetic fibre is made in a factory from chemicals, mostly from petroleum. A blend mixes two or more fibres in one yarn.
explanations.description: Nylon was one of the first fully synthetic fibres. A team led by Wallace Carothers made it in the United States in 1935. Polyester followed, patented in Britain in 1941. To make a filament, the hot liquid is pushed through a plate of very fine holes, the way dough is pushed through an idiyappam press. Polyester and nylon are strong and cheap, dry fast and hardly crease. They take in very little water, so they feel sticky in hot weather. Near a flame they melt and stick to skin, which is why cotton is safer in the kitchen. Viscose, also called rayon, is made from wood or bamboo. The plant cellulose is dissolved and pushed out as new filaments. Elastane is a synthetic fibre that stretches to several times its length. A little of it in socks and leggings makes them cling. Under all these differences, every fibre is built the same way. Its molecules are very long chains, lying mostly along the fibre. Cotton's chains are cellulose, which the plant builds from air, water and sunlight. Wool and silk are chains of protein. Polyester's chains are built in a factory.
examples: A label that says 65% polyester and 35% cotton names a blend. The cotton soaks up sweat, and the polyester adds strength and dries fast.
A nylon school bag keeps books drier in rain than a cotton bag, because nylon takes in very little water.
Most cloth sold as bamboo is viscose made from bamboo, so it is partly natural and partly factory-made.
explanations.art: A factory nozzle with many fine holes pushing out shiny filaments, drawn beside a hand pressing idiyappam dough through a brass press.

explanations.concept: Weaving and stitching by other animals
explanations.definition: Many animals make thread or build with it. Birds weave and stitch nests, spiders and caterpillars spin silk, and weaver ants join leaves with silk.
explanations.description: A male baya weaver tears long strips from paddy, grass or palm leaves. He nicks the leaf with his beak and flies off, holding the strip. He knots the first strips around a thin twig, often on a thorny tree or a palm over water. Then he weaves strips in and out to make a ring, a roof and a round chamber. One nest is said to take up to 500 trips and about 18 days. When the nest is half built, females come to look at it. If a female accepts the nest, the male finishes it with a long entrance tube that hangs down. A tailorbird pierces the edges of a large living leaf with their beak. They pull plant fibre, cotton fluff or spider silk through the holes. The ends fluff out like rivets and hold without a knot. Weaver ants, the red ants of mango trees, pull leaves together in living chains. Other workers carry larvae, who give out silk that glues the leaves. Young weaver birds weave badly at first and improve with practice, as careful studies of African weaver birds showed.
examples: Baya nests hang from babul trees and palms beside paddy fields in much of India.
The common tailorbird lives in gardens in almost every Indian city and calls 'towit, towit' loudly.
A leaf nest of weaver ants on a mango or jackfruit tree is white inside with larval silk.
explanations.art: A male baya weaver, yellow-headed, hanging under a half-built grass nest with a strip in his beak, while a brown female looks on from a twig.

explanations.concept: Five ways to put a pattern into cloth
explanations.definition: A pattern can be woven in, dyed into the threads before weaving, dyed into the finished cloth, printed or painted on, or stitched on.
explanations.description: Woven in: the weaver uses coloured threads on the loom. In a Kanchipuram silk sari, the border and the body are woven in different colours and locked together. In jamdani from Bengal, the weaver adds each flower by hand with extra weft threads. Dyed threads: in ikat, bundles of thread are tied tightly in places and dyed, so the tied parts stay undyed. When the threads are woven, the pattern appears with soft edges. In the patola of Patan, both the warp and the weft are dyed in this way and must meet exactly. Dyed cloth: in bandhani, thousands of tiny points of the cloth are pinched and tied before dyeing. Printed or painted: in ajrakh from Kutch, carved wooden blocks print the cloth in many stages. In kalamkari from Srikalahasti, the artist draws with a bamboo pen. Stitched: embroidery adds the pattern with a needle, as in chikankari from Lucknow, kasuti from Karnataka and Toda embroidery from the Nilgiris.
examples: In Paper Ikat, a shape drawn on the strips before weaving shows up broken into small squares after weaving.
Turn a printed cloth over and the pattern is fainter on the back. Turn a woven check over and it looks the same.
A kasuti pattern is planned so well that it looks the same on both sides of the cloth.
explanations.art: Five small cloth squares in a row: a woven check, a blurred ikat diamond, a field of bandhani dots, a block-printed flower and an embroidered star.

explanations.definition: A handloom is worked by a person. A power loom is driven by a motor. Khadi is cloth that is both spun and woven by hand.
explanations.description: For many centuries, Indian handwoven cotton was sold across Asia, Africa and Europe. In the 1700s and 1800s, machines for spinning and weaving were built in Britain. Mill cloth became cheap, British rule taxed and blocked Indian cloth, and lakhs of spinners and weavers lost their work. The Swadeshi movement began on 7 August 1905 and asked Indians to buy cloth made in India. Later Gandhi asked people to spin on the charkha and wear khadi. Today most cloth in India comes from power looms and mills. A power loom weaves many metres in the time a handloom weaves one. Still, about 35 lakh people work in handloom weaving, and about 7 in every 10 of them are women. The 7th of August is National Handloom Day. People do not agree on what should happen to handloom, and each side has real evidence.
examples: A Kanchipuram silk sari can take a weaver from about ten days to many weeks. A power loom copy takes far less time.
The Jacquard loom of 1804 used cards with punched holes to lift the right threads for a pattern. Early computers borrowed the idea.
A khadi shop sells cloth whose yarn was spun on a charkha and woven on a handloom.

perspectives.explanation: My loom needs no electricity, and I can weave patterns no machine weaves well. But the work is slow, and I earn too little unless buyers pay for the skill.
Machines make cloth that poor families can afford. Without mills, a simple shirt would cost many days' wages.
I buy mill cloth for everyday wear and handloom for what I will keep for years. Both have a place, if weavers are paid fairly.

explanations.art: A split picture: on the left a woman weaving at a wooden handloom, on the right a row of fast power looms in a shed.

explanations.definition: Old cloth can be worn longer, mended, passed on, remade into something else, or broken down into fibre and spun again.
explanations.description: Making cloth uses land, water and energy. Growing the cotton for one T-shirt takes a great deal of water. Estimates range from hundreds to thousands of litres. So the best use of a garment is to wear it for a long time. After that comes passing it on, and then remaking it into something new. Many Indian homes do this without calling it recycling. Old saris become kantha quilts in Bengal, godhadi quilts in Maharashtra and kaudi quilts in Karnataka. Strips of old cloth are woven into chindi rugs. Worn banians become dusters, and old cotton becomes lamp wicks. Last comes true recycling. At Panipat in Haryana, old woollen clothes from many countries are sorted by colour, torn back into fibre and spun into yarn for blankets. Each round of tearing shortens the fibres, so recycled yarn is weaker. Polyester can be melted and spun again, and some polyester is made from used plastic bottles. One problem is still being studied. When synthetic clothes are washed, they shed microfibres that pass into rivers and the sea.
examples: In The Sweater That Went Back to Wool, a sweater is unravelled and knitted again in a smaller size.
In many cities, traders give steel vessels in exchange for old clothes and sell the clothes at second-hand markets.
The Chindi Coaster in this unit is woven from strips of an old T-shirt.

perspectives.explanation: Plastic microfibres are now found in sea water, fish and salt. We should cut them down now, before the harm is fully measured.
Cotton sheds fibres too, and growing cotton takes much water and pesticide. A polyester shirt that lasts ten years may do less harm than three cotton ones.

perspectives.who: A woman who sorts old clothes at Panipat
perspectives.explanation: Cloth that reaches us clean, dry and of one fibre becomes yarn again. Blends and dirty cloth mostly become stuffing or waste.

explanations.art: A ladder with five steps drawn beside a pile of old clothes: wear longer, mend, pass on, remake, recycle.

agreed.text: Woven cloth is held together only by friction where its threads cross. Nothing in it is glued or tied.
agreed.evidence: A single thread can be pulled out of a handkerchief whole. A thread that crosses more threads needs a harder pull, because friction acts at every crossing.

agreed.text: The way a thread is arranged changes what the cloth does, even when the fibre is the same.
agreed.evidence: Cotton woven into a handkerchief hardly stretches. The same cotton knitted into a T-shirt stretches by a quarter of its length or more, and springs back.

agreed.text: People were twisting fibres into string and weaving them tens of thousands of years ago.
agreed.evidence: Fired clay from Pavlov in the Czech Republic, about 26,000 years old, carries the prints of woven cloth and nets. Cloth rots, but a print in baked clay stays.

agreed.text: People in the Indian subcontinent used cotton thread about 7,000 to 8,000 years ago.
agreed.evidence: In 2002, a team led by Christophe Moulherat studied a copper bead from a grave at Mehrgarh. Metal salts had kept the shape of the thread inside, and under a microscope the fibres were cotton.

agreed.text: Clothes made of polyester, nylon and acrylic shed tiny fibres when they are washed, and these reach the sea.
agreed.evidence: In 2011, Mark Browne and his team found such fibres in sand from 18 beaches on six continents. In their washing tests, one garment gave off more than 1,900 fibres in one wash.

agreed.text: A male baya weaver builds the nest, and a female chooses whether to accept it.
agreed.evidence: Watchers from Salim Ali onwards have seen females visit half-built nests, tug at them and sit in them. A male whose nest is refused often leaves it and starts another.

challenging.claim: Only our own kind of human could make string.
challenging.for: String needs planning: fibres must be found, twisted and then twisted together again. Old string almost never survives, so none was known from other humans.
challenging.against: In 2020, Bruce Hardy and his team reported a tiny piece of three-ply cord on a stone tool from Abri du Maras in France. It is more than 40,000 years old and was made by Neanderthals.
challenging.context: This card is about who made the first string. A find in France changed the answer.

challenging.claim: A female baya chooses the male who weaves the neatest nest.
challenging.who: A common belief, found in many books
challenging.for: Females do visit nests, tug at the strips and sit inside before they accept. Young males build rough nests and are often refused.
challenging.against: In 2006, Suhel Quader studied many baya nests in India. Where a nest hung predicted its success a little better than how it was built. This fits females choosing by place more than by weaving.
challenging.context: This card is about how a female baya weaver chooses a nest. A study in India tested a common belief.

challenging.claim: Natural fibres are always better for the Earth than synthetic ones.
challenging.for: Cotton, wool and jute rot back into soil. Polyester comes from petroleum, lasts for centuries and sheds plastic microfibres.
challenging.against: Cotton needs a great deal of water and often much pesticide. A polyester garment that is worn for many years may use less land and water than several cotton ones.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief when people choose clothes. The evidence points both ways.

challenging.claim: People began to wear clothes only a few thousand years ago.
challenging.who: A reasonable guess, because the oldest cloth ever found is only a few thousand years old
challenging.for: Cloth, skins and thread rot, so very old clothes are not found.
challenging.against: The body louse lives only in clothing. Their DNA shows that they split from the head louse at least 83,000 years ago, so people were wearing clothes by then.
challenging.context: This card is about how long people have worn clothes. The evidence comes from an insect.

challenging.claim: Handloom weaving will die out, because machines are faster and cheaper.
challenging.who: Some economists, for more than a hundred years
challenging.for: The number of handloom workers in India has fallen over the last thirty years, and many weavers' children choose other work.
challenging.against: Handloom has outlived this forecast since the 1800s. Some cloth, such as jamdani and double ikat, is still made well only by hand, and buyers pay for it.
challenging.context: This card is about the future of handloom weaving in India. People have argued about it since the first mills.

challenging.claim: Silk can be made without harming any moth.
challenging.who: Sellers of ahimsa silk, also called peace silk
challenging.for: The moths are allowed to come out of their cocoons alive, and the broken cocoons are spun afterwards.
challenging.against: The moths cannot fly or feed and live only a few days. Far more eggs hatch than a farm can feed, so many caterpillars still die.
challenging.context: This card is about silk made after the moths leave their cocoons. People disagree on how much kinder it is.

big_questions.q: A woven cloth has no glue and no knots. So what holds millions of threads together?
big_questions.hint: Pull one thread out of an old handkerchief. Feel where the pull resists. Then think about what happens at each crossing.

big_questions.q: A sweater is unravelled into a ball of wool, and no wool is lost. Is the sweater gone, or is it still there in the wool?
big_questions.hint: Ask what a sweater is: the wool, or the way the wool is arranged. Could it be both?

big_questions.q: In ikat, the pattern is dyed into loose threads before any cloth exists. Is the pattern in the thread or in the cloth?
big_questions.hint: Think about Paper Ikat. Could you see the shape on one strip alone? What had to happen before it showed?

big_questions.q: A young baya weaves a rough nest and an older one weaves a fine nest. Is weaving something a baya knows, or something a baya learns?
big_questions.hint: Think about your own first running stitches. What did you know before you began, and what came only with practice?

big_questions.q: How many living beings and people had a hand in the shirt you are wearing?
big_questions.hint: Start with the cotton plant and the soil. Count the farmer, the spinner, the weaver or knitter, the dyer, the tailor and the seller.

big_questions.q: A machine weaves a sari in hours, and a person takes two weeks. Both saris are cloth. What is different about them?
big_questions.hint: Think about the cloth, the price, who earns from it and what is lost if no one remembers how.

story.title: The Sweater That Went Back to Wool
story.note: A made-up story. Thenmozhi, Kathir and Paati are imagined, and so is their house in Kotagiri, a real town in the Nilgiri hills of Tamil Nadu. The cloth facts are real. A cut across knitted cloth gives short pieces of yarn and loose loops that run into a ladder. A knitted sweater can be unravelled into yarn, and many families steam the crinkled yarn straight over a pot and knit a new sweater.
text: In Kotagiri, the mist comes up the tea slopes in December and sits in the lanes until ten in the morning. Thenmozhi was eleven that winter. Her brother Kathir was six, and he had no sweater. He had left it on the school bus in November, and the bus had not given it back.

"He can have my red one," Thenmozhi told Paati. The red sweater had been hers since Class 2. It was tight across her shoulders now and stopped above her wrists. On Kathir it was the other way round. The body was nearly right, but the sleeves hung past his fingers like two red socks.
"Leave it on the chair," Paati said. "I will see to it on Sunday." Paati was shelling peas, and she did not look up.

Thenmozhi did not want to wait until Sunday. In October she had watched the tailor near the bus stand shorten her school pinafore. He had cut a strip off the bottom, folded the new edge up and run it under his machine. It had taken him four minutes. A sleeve, she thought, was only a small pinafore.
She measured Kathir's arm with the tape from Paati's tin. She marked each sleeve with chalk, eight centimetres from the end. Then she took the big scissors and cut both sleeves straight across.

The cut edges looked wrong at once. They were not flat, like the pinafore's edge. Each was a row of tiny open loops, and between the loops sat short red crumbs of wool, none longer than her finger. She brushed the crumbs off, and more came. She folded the edge to hem it. The loops slipped out of the fold. She pulled the sleeve gently to make it lie flat, and one loop let go, and then the loop under it, and the one under that. A thin gap ran up the sleeve towards the elbow, with little bars of wool across it like the rungs of a ladder.
Thenmozhi put the sweater down very carefully, the way you put down something that might still be falling.

After a while she looked again. A loose end of wool stuck out at the cut edge. She pulled it. A whole row came away with a soft ticking feeling, loop after loop, from the seam all the way round the sleeve and back to the seam. There the wool turned and went into the next row.

She held the pulled-out wool against the tape. It was crinkled like a tiny noodle, and when she drew it straight, it was sixty-two centimetres long. She put the tape around the sleeve. Twenty centimetres. One row was three times as long as the sleeve was round.

So where did the extra wool go? She looked closely at the open loops. The wool did not run straight round the sleeve. It went up, over, down and under, up, over, down and under, all the way round. And the crumbs on the floor were pieces of that same wool. Her scissors had gone through it again and again.
"Paati," she said. "I have done something to the red sweater."
Paati came and looked at the two cut sleeves, the ladder and the heap of crumbs. She was quiet for a moment.

"A pinafore is woven," Paati said. "Hundreds of threads cross each other, and each one is held by all the rest. Cut some, and the others stay where they are. This is knitted. I knit my sleeves from the shoulder down, so that I can add to them when a child grows. I began this one with one thread and looped it back and forth until I reached the wrist."
"One thread," said Thenmozhi. "And I cut it in a great many places."
"You did," said Paati.
Thenmozhi looked at the end of wool still in her hand. She had pulled out three whole rows by now. The wool lay in her lap, crinkled, red and unbroken, longer than she was tall.
"Paati," she said slowly. "If it is one thread, then I do not need to cut it at all. I can pull all of it out. The whole sweater. Then it is just wool again, and you can knit it small."
Paati smiled then, for the first time. "That is what I was going to do on Sunday," she said. "You have saved me the start."

They worked until dark. Paati snipped the stitches that joined the sleeves to the body, because a sweater is knitted in pieces and sewn together. Then Thenmozhi pulled. Each piece came undone from the end where Paati had finished it, row by row, and Kathir walked backwards across the room holding the end. They wound the wool around the back of a chair. It was as crinkled as instant noodles.
"It remembers being a sweater," said Kathir.

"It will forget in the steam," said Paati. She tied each loop of wool in four places and held it over the idli pot until the kinks went soft. Then she hung the loops from the window bar, with a steel tumbler tied to the bottom of each one to pull it straight.
By morning the wool was smooth. There were four fat balls of it, two short lengths from the cut-off ends, and a small paper bag of red crumbs.
"Those are the price of the scissors," said Paati. "Too short to knit. Keep them. They will stuff a ball for the cat."

Paati knitted for nine evenings, and Thenmozhi knitted the plain rows when Paati's eyes were tired. The new sweater was smaller in every direction, so one ball of wool was left over. Kathir wore it to school on the first day of January, with the sleeves ending exactly at his wrists.
"It is my sweater," he told everybody.
"It is my sweater's wool," said Thenmozhi. "That is not quite the same thing."
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story turns when Thenmozhi measures one row of wool and finds it three times as long as the sleeve is round. A knitted sweater is one thread in loops, so a cut goes through that thread again and again, and the loops beside the cut can run. A woven pinafore is many threads that hold each other, so it can be cut and hemmed. The same fact that spoils the cut also saves the day. Because the sweater is one thread, the whole of it can go back to being wool.
ask: Why could the tailor cut and hem the pinafore, when the same cut spoiled the sweater sleeve?
One row of wool was 62 centimetres long, but the sleeve was only 20 centimetres round. What did that tell Thenmozhi?
At the end, Thenmozhi says it is her sweater's wool, and not quite her sweater. What do you think she means?
Which old thing in your home could be taken apart and made into something else?

games.title: Woven, Dyed, Printed or Stitched? The cloth of India cards
games.context: This is a card game about 24 cloth traditions from many parts of India. Each card says how a cloth is made. You decide how its pattern got there: woven in, dyed into the threads, dyed into the cloth, printed or painted, or stitched on.

printables.title: 24 cloth cards to cut out (the answer and the place are on the back)

items.f: Kanchipuram silk sari. The border and the body are woven in different colours and locked together on the loom, using three shuttles.
Jamdani. The weaver adds each small flower by hand with extra weft threads, while weaving very fine cotton.
items.b: Woven in. West Bengal, and Dhaka in Bangladesh (East).

items.f: Paithani sari. Peacocks and parrots are built up on the loom from many coloured silk wefts, and look the same on both sides.
items.b: Woven in. Paithan and Yeola, Maharashtra (West).

items.f: Kasavu. Cream cotton cloth is woven with a border of golden thread, and worn at Onam.
Ilkal sari. The body and the end piece have separate warp threads, joined on the loom by small loops, thread by thread.
Kani shawl. Fine goat hair is woven with dozens of small wooden sticks, each carrying one colour of weft.
Bhavani jamakkalam. Thick cotton floor spreads are woven in broad, bright stripes on pit looms.
Pattamadai mat. Korai grass is split very fine and woven across cotton warp threads into a mat as soft as cloth.
Pochampally ikat. Bundles of thread are tied and dyed before weaving, so the diamonds have feathered edges.
Patola. Both the warp and the weft are tied and dyed before weaving, and must meet exactly. One sari takes many months.
Sambalpuri sari. Threads are tied and dyed before weaving, to make shells, wheels and flowers with soft edges.
Bandhani. Thousands of tiny points of the cloth are pinched and tied with thread. Then the cloth is dyed, and the points stay as dots.
items.b: Cloth tied and dyed. Gujarat and Rajasthan (West).

items.f: Sungudi sari. Cotton saris are tied in small dots and dyed, a craft of the Saurashtrian weavers of Madurai.
items.b: Cloth tied and dyed. Madurai, Tamil Nadu (South).

items.f: Leheriya. The cloth is rolled from corner to corner, tied at gaps and dyed, which leaves slanting wavy stripes.
Ajrakh. Carved wooden blocks print the cloth in many stages, with indigo blue and madder red, often on both sides.
Kalamkari of Srikalahasti. The artist draws on the cloth by hand with a bamboo pen and plant dyes.
Bagru print. Wooden blocks print the cloth with plant dyes, and a mud paste keeps the dye off some parts.
Kantha. Layers of old saris and dhotis are joined with rows and rows of running stitch.
items.b: Stitched on. West Bengal and Odisha (East).

items.f: Chikankari. White thread is stitched on fine white cloth, over a pattern first stamped in washable blue.
Phulkari. Bright silk thread is stitched from the back of coarse cotton cloth, by counting its threads.
Toda embroidery. Toda women stitch red and black patterns on cream cotton by counting threads, with no drawing.
items.b: Stitched on. The Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu (South).

items.f: Kasuti. The pattern is stitched by counting threads, with no knots, and looks the same on both sides.
Lambani embroidery. Lambani women stitch bright patches, small mirrors and shells on to cloth.
Khneng embroidery. A few Khasi women stitch a pattern like the legs of a centipede on eri silk shawls.

check.q: How is ikat different from bandhani?
options: Ikat ties and dyes threads, bandhani ties and dyes cloth
Ikat is printed, bandhani is stitched
They are two names for one craft
check.why: In ikat the threads are tied and dyed before weaving, so the pattern appears as the cloth is woven. In bandhani the cloth is woven first, then pinched, tied and dyed.

games.title: Fibre Detective: three clues, one fibre
games.context: This is a guessing game about 12 fibres. Each card gives three clues, from hard to easy. You name the fibre with as few clues as you can.

items.f: Clue 1: I grow as hairs on a seed, and each of my fibres is one cell. Clue 2: I take in water easily, so towels and banians are made of me. Clue 3: I am picked from white bolls on a plant.
Clue 1: Farmers soak my stems in water for two or three weeks to free me. Clue 2: India grows more of me than any other country, mostly in Bengal. Clue 3: Gunny sacks are made of me.
items.b: Jute, a plant fibre from a stem.

items.f: Clue 1: I come from the husk of a fruit that can float across the sea. Clue 2: Water does not rot me quickly, so I make boat ropes and doormats. Clue 3: Alappuzha in Kerala is famous for me.
items.b: Coir, the fibre of the coconut husk.

items.f: Clue 1: I come from the stem of the flax plant. Clue 2: I am cool and crisp, and I crease easily. Clue 3: My name begins with L, and summer shirts are made of me.
items.b: Linen, a plant fibre from a stem.

items.f: Clue 1: Each of my fibres is wavy and covered with tiny scales. Clue 2: I trap still air, so I keep a body warm. Clue 3: I am sheared from sheep.
Clue 1: I am combed out, not cut, from an under-coat in spring. Clue 2: My goat lives above 4,000 metres in Ladakh. Clue 3: The finest shawls of Kashmir are woven from me.
items.b: Pashmina, the under-hair of the Changthangi goat.

items.f: Clue 1: I am one filament, many hundreds of metres long. Clue 2: My maker eats only mulberry leaves. Clue 3: Kanchipuram and Mysuru saris are woven from me.
items.b: Mulberry silk, an animal fibre from a caterpillar's cocoon.

items.f: Clue 1: My caterpillars eat castor leaves. Clue 2: My cocoon is open at one end, so I am spun and not unwound. Clue 3: I come from Assam and Meghalaya, and some people call me ahimsa silk.
Clue 1: I am golden without any dye. Clue 2: My moths live in the Brahmaputra valley. Clue 3: Assam is famous for me.
Clue 1: I was first made in 1935, one of the first fully synthetic fibres. Clue 2: I am made from petroleum, and I melt near a flame. Clue 3: Toothbrush bristles and fishing lines are made of me.
Clue 1: Some of me is made from used plastic bottles. Clue 2: I take in very little water, so I dry fast. Clue 3: Most sports jerseys are made of me.
Clue 1: I begin as wood or bamboo, but a factory dissolves me and makes me into filaments. Clue 2: I am smooth and was once sold as 'artificial silk'. Clue 3: Labels call me viscose or rayon.
items.b: Viscose, also called rayon: plant cellulose remade in a factory.

Wool
Nylon

experiments.title: Woven or Knitted: which cloth stretches more, and where does the stretch come from?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hang the same bottle of water from a strip of woven cotton and from two strips of knitted cotton. You measure how much each strip stretches. Then you pull out single threads to find out where the stretch comes from.
experiments.question: Under the same pull, does knitted cotton stretch more than woven cotton? If it does, where does the extra length come from?
experiments.predict: Guess first. A strip of handkerchief cloth and a strip of T-shirt cloth each carry the same bottle of water. Which strip will stretch more? Will the T-shirt cloth stretch the same amount along the shirt and across the shirt? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: All three strips are cotton. Each is 4 cm wide, with two pen marks 20 cm apart. The same bottle hangs from each strip for the same 10 seconds. Only the way the thread is arranged changes. Read the T-shirt's label first. If it lists elastane, spandex or Lycra, choose another T-shirt, because that fibre stretches by itself.
results_table: After the bottle is taken out (cm)

materials.item: an old woven cotton cloth that can be cut, such as a handkerchief, a pillow cover or a cotton dupatta
an old knitted cotton T-shirt or banian that can be cut, adult size if possible, with no elastane on the label
a 500 ml bottle full of water with the cap on tight (about half a kilogram)
a carry bag with two handles
a door handle, a window grill bar or a strong hook, at about the child's shoulder height
scissors, a ruler and a ball pen
a pin or a needle for picking out threads, kept in a bar of soap

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the cutting. Keep feet clear of the hanging bottle, in case a knot slips. Stick the pin in a bar of soap whenever it is not in use.

schedule.what: Cut three strips. Hang the bottle from each and measure the stretch. Pull out one woven thread and one knitted thread and measure them. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for the stretch of each strip. Under it, write the length of the woven thread and the knitted thread you pulled out. Then write one sentence for your claim, one for your evidence and one for your reasoning.

Write 'along' on it. 3. Cut a ring 4 cm wide right around the body of the T-shirt. 4. Cut the ring open and trim it to 40 cm. Write 'across' on it. 5. Keep the leftover cloth for later.
flow.say: We need three strips of cloth, all the same size. One strip is woven. The other two are knitted. We cut them in two different directions.
flow.kid: Cut three strips with a grown-up. Each is 4 cm wide and 40 cm long. Label the T-shirt strips 'along' and 'across'.
flow.parent: The knitted strips curl into tubes at the edges. That is normal for T-shirt cloth. Write the labels near one end, where the knot will be.
flow.context: This step of Woven or Knitted cuts three strips of the same size: one woven, and two knitted in different directions.

flow.do: 1. Lay the woven strip flat. Draw two pen marks 20 cm apart, in the middle of the strip. 2. Tie one end to the door handle. Tie the other end through both handles of the empty carry bag. 3. Measure between the marks and write it down. 4. Lower the bottle gently into the bag. Wait 10 seconds and measure again. 5. Take the bottle out and measure once more.
flow.say: First the woven strip. Watch the two marks when the bottle goes in. Do they move apart?
flow.kid: Mark two lines 20 cm apart. Tie the strip to the handle and the bag. Measure. Put the bottle in. Wait 10 seconds. Measure again.
flow.parent: Tie firm double knots. Measure with the ruler held beside the strip, not pressed on it. Expect the woven marks to move apart by only a few millimetres.
flow.context: This step of Woven or Knitted hangs a bottle of water from the woven strip and measures how far two marks move apart.

flow.do: 1. Do the same with the knitted strip marked 'along'. 2. Do the same with the knitted strip marked 'across'. 3. For each strip, take away 20 from the length with the bottle. That is the stretch. 4. Write all the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Now the two knitted strips. Which one stretches more? Does each strip go back when the bottle comes out?
flow.kid: Test the 'along' strip. Then test the 'across' strip. Write each stretch. Does each strip go back afterwards?

ask.q: What did the knitted strips do that the woven strip did not?
good: They grew several centimetres longer.
They became narrower as they stretched.
They went most of the way back when the bottle came out.

flow.parent: Knitted strips usually stretch by a few centimetres along the shirt and by much more across it. Results differ from one T-shirt to another.
flow.context: This step of Woven or Knitted hangs the same bottle from two knitted strips, one cut along the T-shirt and one cut across it.

flow.do: 1. Cut a piece 5 cm wide from the leftover woven cloth. Pull one thread out of it, right across. 2. Lay the thread straight beside the ruler and measure it. 3. Cut a piece of T-shirt cloth 5 cm wide, across the shirt. 4. With the pin, pick loose bits off one cut edge until a single thread runs all the way across. 5. Pull that thread out, hold it straight without stretching it, and measure it.
flow.say: Now take a piece of the woven cloth and a piece of the knitted cloth, each 5 cm wide. We will pull one thread out of each. Then we will see how long a thread each piece holds across that width.
flow.kid: Cut a piece 5 cm wide from each cloth. Pull one thread right across each piece. Measure both threads.

ask.q: The knitted thread is much longer than 5 cm. Where was all that thread, inside a piece only 5 cm wide?
good: It was bent into loops.
It went up and down in loops, not straight across.

flow.parent: Expect a little over 5 cm for the woven thread and about 15 to 20 cm for the knitted thread. If the knitted thread will not run, try the opposite cut edge. If it keeps breaking, use an old sock or sweater, whose yarn is thicker.
flow.context: This step of Woven or Knitted pulls one thread out of each cloth, to compare how much thread crosses 5 cm of cloth.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. 2. Draw the bar chart of the three stretches. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Use the thread lengths in your reason.
flow.kid: Say what you guessed and what you saw. Then say why it happened. Use your thread lengths.

check.q: In Woven or Knitted, why did the knitted cotton stretch more than the woven cotton?
options: The knitted cotton is a softer kind of cotton
The knitted thread runs in loops, which can open out
The woven strip was cut wider
check.why: Both cloths are cotton, and the strips were the same width. The knitted thread runs in loops, so a row holds 3 or 4 times as much thread as the cloth is wide. A pull opens the loops out. If you chose 'softer cotton', look again at the two threads you measured.

flow.context: This is the last step of Woven or Knitted. Here you explain the stretch, using the lengths of the threads you pulled out.

experiments.title: The Leaky Seam Test: how small must a stitch be to hold mustard seeds?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sew three seams with long, medium and short running stitches. You stretch each seam over a tumbler, rub mustard seeds across it, and count how many fall through.
experiments.question: Does the length of a stitch change how many seeds get through a seam? How short must a stitch be to stop a mustard seed?
experiments.predict: Guess first. One seam has stitches 1 cm long. One has stitches half a centimetre long. One has stitches a quarter of a centimetre long. Through which seam will the most mustard seeds fall? Will any seam let none through? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: All three seams are 8 cm long, in the same cloth, sewn with the same thread, 1 cm from the edge. Each seam is stretched flat over the same tumbler. The same spoonful of seeds is rubbed across each seam 20 times. Only the length of the stitch changes.

materials.item: old plain cotton cloth, such as a pillow cover or a bedsheet, cut into pieces 10 cm by 8 cm
a sewing needle with a large eye
strong sewing thread in a colour that shows on the cloth
mustard seeds (kadugu or rai)
raw rice
a steel tumbler about 7 cm across at the mouth, and a rubber band that fits tightly round it
a steel plate, a small bowl, a ruler, a ball pen, scissors and a phone timer
a bar of soap to hold the needle

experiments.safety: A needle is sharp. Sit at a table to sew, and push the needle away from your other hand. Stick the needle in the bar of soap whenever it is not in use. Count the needles at the start and at the end.

schedule.what: Mark and sew three seams with long, medium and short stitches, timing each. Stretch each seam over a tumbler and count the seeds that fall through.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each seam, showing the mustard seeds that fell through. Then write one sentence for your claim, one for your evidence and one for your reasoning.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: mustard seeds that fell through each seam
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three small pieces of white cloth, each with a pen line 1 cm from one long edge and dots along the line: wide apart on the first, closer on the second, closest on the third.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line on three pieces. Mark dots 1 cm apart on piece A, and half a cm apart on pieces B and C.

setup.art: A child sewing a running stitch through two layers of cloth with dark thread, the needle going down at one dot and up at the next, a bar of soap with a spare needle beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Sew each seam through two layers with a running stitch.

setup.art: The two sewn pieces opened like a book and stretched over a steel tumbler with a rubber band, the seam running across the middle like a tiny ladder.
setup.caption: 3. Open the pieces and stretch the seam flat over a tumbler.

setup.art: A finger rubbing mustard seeds across the seam on top of the tumbler, with a few seeds visible inside the tumbler below.
setup.caption: 4. Rub the seeds across the seam 20 times. Count the seeds inside the tumbler.

flow.do: 1. On three pieces of cloth, draw a line 1 cm from one long edge. Start and end the line 1 cm from the short edges, so it is 8 cm long. 2. On piece A, mark a dot every 1 cm along the line. 3. On pieces B and C, mark a dot every half centimetre. 4. Ask for the guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: Seam A will have stitches 1 cm long. Seam B will have half that. Seam C will have a quarter. Which seam will leak the most seeds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a line on three pieces. Mark the dots. Which seam will leak the most seeds? Why? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Long stitches leave long gaps between the needle holes.
A seed can only get through a gap that is bigger than the seed.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaky Seam Test. Here you mark three pieces of cloth for long, medium and short stitches, and guess which seam will leak most.

flow.do: 1. Lay piece A on a plain piece, with the edges matching. 2. Thread the needle, double the thread and knot the end. 3. Start the timer. Sew through both layers: down at one dot and up at the next. 4. Pull the thread until it lies flat, without gathering the cloth. 5. At the end, sew two small stitches on the same spot and cut the thread. 6. Stop the timer and write the minutes.
flow.say: Go down at one dot and up at the next. Keep the thread flat. I will time you.
flow.kid: Put piece A on a plain piece. Sew down at one dot and up at the next. Finish with two stitches on one spot.
flow.parent: If your child has never sewn, do the Stitch Sampler activity first. Seam A has 8 stitches.
flow.context: This step of the Leaky Seam Test sews seam A, which has running stitches 1 cm long, and times the sewing.

flow.do: 1. Sew seam B in the same way, through every dot. It has 16 stitches. Time it. 2. Sew seam C through every dot and once more halfway between each pair of dots. It has 32 stitches. Time it. 3. Write both times in the table.
flow.say: Seam B has twice as many stitches as seam A. Seam C has twice as many again. How long do you think each will take?
flow.kid: Sew seam B through every dot. Sew seam C through every dot and once in between. Time each seam.
flow.parent: If time is short, sew seam C yourself while your child sews seam B. Time it all the same. The tiny stitches of seam C are slow, and that slowness is one of the results.
flow.context: This step of the Leaky Seam Test sews seam B, with stitches half a centimetre long, and seam C, with stitches a quarter of a centimetre long.

flow.do: 1. Open the two pieces of seam A like a book. Lay them over the tumbler with the seam across the middle and the two short flaps hanging inside. 2. Put the rubber band round the rim. Pull the cloth edges down gently until the cloth is flat. 3. Look at the seam. Can you see gaps between the stitches? 4. Stand the tumbler on the plate and pour the teaspoon of mustard seeds on the cloth. 5. With one finger, rub the seeds across the seam and back 20 times. 6. Tip the seeds from the top into the bowl. Lift off the cloth and count the seeds inside the tumbler. 7. Do the same for seams B and C.
flow.say: Look at the seam before the seeds go on. What do you see between the stitches? Now rub the seeds across it 20 times.
flow.kid: Stretch the seam over the tumbler. Look for gaps. Rub the mustard seeds across 20 times. Count the seeds inside the tumbler.

ask.q: What does seam A look like when it is stretched flat?
good: Like a ladder: the thread makes rungs and there are gaps between them.
The two cloths pull apart between the needle holes.

flow.parent: Pull each cloth equally flat, like a drum skin and no tighter. Seam A usually lets many seeds through and seam C none or almost none. If no seeds fall through seam A, the cloth is too slack: pull it flatter and try again.
flow.context: This step of the Leaky Seam Test stretches each seam over a tumbler, rubs mustard seeds across it and counts the seeds that fall through.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess what rice will do. 2. Repeat the test on all three seams with 1 level teaspoon of raw rice. 3. Write the counts in the table.
flow.say: A rice grain is longer than a mustard seed. Will more rice get through, or less? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Now try rice. Guess first: will more get through, or less? Why? Test all three seams.
flow.parent: Rice usually gets through far less than mustard, because a long grain must meet the gap end on. Whatever you find is a real result. Write it down as it is.
flow.context: This step of the Leaky Seam Test repeats the test with rice, to see whether the size and shape of a grain matter.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. 2. Look at the table together: stitch length, number of stitches, minutes and seeds. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me what the shortest stitches cost you.
flow.kid: Say what you guessed and what you saw. Then say why it happened. What did short stitches cost you?

check.q: In the Leaky Seam Test, why did the seam with 1 cm stitches let the most seeds through?
options: Its thread was thinner
The cloth can open between needle holes that are far apart
Mustard seeds are attracted to long stitches
check.why: A running stitch pins the two cloths together only at the needle holes. Between the holes the cloths can pull apart. Holes 1 cm apart leave gaps wide enough for a mustard seed. The thread was the same in all three seams.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Leaky Seam Test. Here you explain your results, and weigh a tight seam against the time it takes to sew.

experiments.title: The Fray Test: which cut edge loses the fewest threads?
experiments.context: In this experiment you cut the same thin cloth in three ways. You add a selvedge and a piece of knitted cloth, and shake them all in a jar of water. Then you measure the fringe of loose threads on each edge.
experiments.question: Which edge of a cloth frays the most when it is washed: a straight cut, a slant cut, a zigzag cut or a selvedge? Does knitted cloth fray at all?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Five kinds of edge go into the same jar of water and are shaken 300 times: a straight cut, a slant cut, a zigzag cut, a selvedge, and a cut edge of T-shirt cloth. Which edge will have the widest fringe of loose threads? Which will have none? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: The three woven pieces are cut from the same cloth, to the same size. All the pieces are shaken together in one jar, so each gets the same water and the same number of shakes. Only the kind of edge changes.

materials.item: thin, loosely woven cotton cloth that can be cut, such as an old dupatta, an old cotton sari, or a thorthu or gamcha towel, with one selvedge edge if possible
materials.qty: a piece about 25 cm by 25 cm

materials.item: a scrap of knitted T-shirt cloth, such as the leftovers from Woven or Knitted
a jar or a box with a tight lid, about 1 litre, half full of water
a square of paper 6 cm by 6 cm, to cut around
scissors, a ball pen, a ruler marked in millimetres and a steel plate

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the cutting. Hold the lid on with one hand while shaking, and shake over a sink or a bucket.

schedule.what: Cut a straight piece, a slant piece and a zigzag piece from one cloth. Shake them in water with a knitted piece 300 times. Measure the fringe on every edge.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for the fringe on each kind of edge. Then write one sentence for your claim, one for your evidence and one for your reasoning.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: fringe after 300 shakes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A thin checked cloth on a table with a paper square laid on it twice: once square to the threads, with one side on the cloth's finished edge, and once turned like a diamond.
setup.caption: 1. Cut one square along the threads and one square on the slant.

setup.art: A third cloth square with small V-shaped teeth cut all round its edges, beside a small square of red T-shirt cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Cut zigzag teeth round a third square. Add a piece of T-shirt cloth.

setup.art: A child shaking a lidded steel box over a sink, with the four cloth pieces and water visible in a cut-away view.
setup.caption: 3. Shake all the pieces in water 300 times.

setup.art: Four wet cloth pieces laid flat on a steel plate, one with a clear fringe along its straight edges, and a ruler held against the fringe.
setup.caption: 4. Lay the pieces flat. Measure the fringe on each edge.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the thin cloth and find its selvedge, the firm edge that was never cut. 2. Explain the three cuts you will make. 3. Ask for the guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: We will cut this cloth straight, on the slant and in zigzags. Which edge will fray most in the wash? Which will not fray at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find the firm edge of the cloth. Which cut edge will fray the most? Which will not fray? Why? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: On a straight cut, the last thread has nothing outside it to hold it in.
The selvedge has no cut ends, so nothing can slide out.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fray Test. Here you find the selvedge of a cloth and guess which kind of edge will fray most.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper square on the cloth with its sides along the threads and one side on the selvedge. Cut round it. Write 1 on the piece. 2. Turn the paper like a diamond, so its corners point along the threads. Cut round it. Write 2. 3. Cut a third square along the threads. Snip small V-shaped teeth, half a centimetre deep, all round its edges. Write 3. 4. Measure any fringe on each piece now and write it in the table.
flow.say: Piece 1 is cut along the threads. Piece 2 is cut on the slant. Piece 3 has zigzag edges. Look closely: where do the threads end on each?
flow.kid: Cut three squares with a grown-up: straight, slant and zigzag. Number them 1, 2 and 3.
flow.parent: If the cloth has no selvedge, leave that row of the table empty. Ball pen marks stay on through the shaking.
flow.context: This step of the Fray Test cuts three squares from the same cloth: one along the threads, one on the slant and one with zigzag edges.

flow.do: 1. Put the three woven pieces and the knitted piece in the jar of water. 2. Close the lid tightly. 3. Shake the jar 300 times, counting aloud. Take turns, 100 shakes each.
flow.say: A washing machine rubs and tumbles cloth. Our jar does the same. Count the shakes with me.
flow.kid: Put all four pieces in the jar. Close the lid tight. Shake 300 times. Count aloud.
flow.context: This step of the Fray Test shakes all the pieces together in a jar of water, as a washing machine would.

flow.do: 1. Lift each piece out and lay it flat on the plate, without pulling its edges. 2. On each edge, measure the fringe at its widest. The fringe is the part where only loose thread ends are left. 3. Write the numbers in the table. 4. Look in the jar for threads that came right out.
flow.say: Lay each piece flat without pulling. Which edge has the widest fringe? Is there any edge with no fringe at all?
flow.kid: Lay the pieces flat. Do not pull the edges. Measure the fringe on each edge in millimetres.

ask.q: What does the cut edge of the knitted piece look like?
good: It has curled up, but it has no fringe.
A few short bits came off, but no long threads.

flow.parent: Expect the widest fringe on the straight cut, clearly less on the slant cut and the zigzag cut, and none on the selvedge. If almost nothing has frayed, the cloth is tightly woven. Shake 300 more times.
flow.context: This step of the Fray Test measures the fringe of loose threads on each kind of edge after the shaking.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. 2. Look at a hemmed edge on a shirt or a kurta together. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then look at the hem on a piece of clothing. What job is it doing?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed and what you saw. Then say why it happened. What does a hem do?

check.q: In the Fray Test, why did the selvedge not fray?
options: It is made of stronger cotton
The cross thread turns back there, so no cut ends exist
It was not in the water
check.why: At the selvedge the weft thread turns round and goes back into the cloth. There are no cut ends, so no thread can slide off. All the edges were in the same water, and the cotton is the same.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fray Test. Here you explain why some edges fray, and what a hem is for.

activities.title: Thread Paths: three cloths under the phone camera
activities.context: In this activity you look very closely at a handkerchief, a T-shirt and a pair of jeans with a phone camera. You draw the path one thread takes in each cloth. It leads to the question of the unit: why does one cotton cloth stretch and another not?

materials.item: a woven cotton handkerchief, or a cotton shirt or pillow cover
a cotton T-shirt or banian
a pair of jeans, or a towel
a phone camera, or a hand lens
plain paper and two colour pencils

activities.record: Draw three boxes. In each, draw the threads of one cloth as you see them on the screen, and colour the path of one thread in red.

setup.art: A phone held a few centimetres above a checked handkerchief on a table, its screen showing the threads crossing over and under.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the phone close to the cloth and zoom in.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three boxes: crossed lines in the first, rows of loops in the second and slanting lines in the third, with one thread coloured red in each.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the path of one thread in each cloth.

flow.do: 1. Lay the handkerchief flat in good light. 2. Hold the phone camera about 5 cm above it. Zoom in and touch the screen to focus. 3. Ask your child to follow one thread across the screen with a fingertip. 4. Draw what you see in the first box.
flow.say: Look at the screen. Follow one thread with your finger. Where does it go when it meets another thread?
flow.kid: Zoom in on the handkerchief. Follow one thread with your finger. Where does it go? Draw it.

ask.q: What does the thread do when it meets another thread?
good: It goes over one and under the next.
The threads cross like a mat.

flow.parent: If the picture is blurred, move the phone a little further away and zoom in more. A hand lens works too.
flow.context: This is the first step of Thread Paths. Here you look closely at a handkerchief and follow the path of one thread.

flow.do: 1. Look at the T-shirt in the same way. Draw it in the second box. 2. Look at the outside of the jeans, then the inside. Draw the outside in the third box.
flow.say: Now the T-shirt. Are the threads crossing, or doing something else? Then look at the jeans. Which way do the lines run?
flow.kid: Zoom in on the T-shirt. Are the threads crossing? Draw them. Then look at the jeans, outside and inside.

ask.q: How is the T-shirt different from the handkerchief?
good: The thread makes rows of small loops, like tiny V shapes.
I cannot see two sets of threads crossing.

flow.parent: T-shirt cloth shows columns of small V shapes. Each V is one loop. Denim shows slanting lines, and it is paler inside because the white threads show more there.
flow.context: This step of Thread Paths looks closely at a T-shirt and a pair of jeans, to compare them with the handkerchief.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to pull the handkerchief gently from side to side, then from top to bottom. 2. Do the same with the T-shirt. 3. Read the labels. If both say cotton, ask the question below. 4. Write down your child's idea. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: Both of these are cotton. One stretches and one hardly moves. What could make the difference? Tell me your idea and your reason.
flow.kid: Pull each cloth gently. Which one stretches? Both are cotton. Why might they differ? Write your idea.
flow.parent: Keep your child's idea. The experiment Woven or Knitted tests it.
flow.context: This is the last step of Thread Paths. Here you pull the two cotton cloths and ask why only one stretches.

activities.title: Take a Thread Apart: plies, twist and fibres
activities.context: In this activity you untwist a piece of thick thread until it opens into thinner strands, and then into single fibres. You find out how short fibres make a long thread, and why threads are made of strands twisted two ways.

materials.item: thick cotton thread, such as a thread pulled from a towel, or white kite thread, or a piece of cotton string
a cotton lamp wick, or a pinch of cotton wool
knitting wool, or any thick yarn
a ruler
a phone camera, or a hand lens

activities.record: Draw the thread, one ply and one fibre side by side. Write the length of each beside it.

setup.art: Two hands holding a short piece of thick white thread, one hand rolling the end so that the thread opens into three thinner strands.
setup.caption: 1. Untwist a thick thread until it opens into plies.

setup.art: One thin strand teased apart into a wisp of fine fibres beside a ruler, with a single fibre about 3 cm long.
setup.caption: 2. Open one ply and measure a single fibre.

setup.art: A length of red wool twisted tight, folded in half and twisting round itself into a two-strand cord.
setup.caption: 3. Twist a yarn, fold it in half and let it go.

flow.do: 1. Hold the thick thread between two hands, about 5 cm apart. 2. Roll one end between finger and thumb until the thread opens. 3. Count the thinner strands. Each one is a ply. 4. Let go, and watch what the thread does.
