flow.say: Roll the end until the thread opens. How many strands is it made of? What happens when you let go?
flow.kid: Roll one end of the thread until it opens. Count the strands. Let go. What happens?

ask.q: What did the thread do when you let go?
good: It twisted itself back together.
The strands wrapped round each other again.

flow.parent: Most thick threads have 2 or 3 plies. Some string has more.
flow.context: This is the first step of Take a Thread Apart. Here you untwist a thick thread and count the plies inside it.

flow.do: 1. Separate one ply and untwist it the other way until it turns fluffy. 2. Pull out one single fibre and lay it beside the ruler. 3. Measure it. 4. Pull the lamp wick gently apart and notice how little force it takes.
flow.say: Now open one ply. Can you pull out a single fibre? How long is it? Our thread is 15 cm long. How can such short fibres make it?
flow.kid: Untwist one strand until it is fluffy. Pull out one fibre. Measure it. How can short fibres make a long thread?

ask.q: The fibres are only 2 or 3 cm long. What stops the thread from sliding apart?
good: The twist presses the fibres together.
Friction between the fibres holds them, as long as they are twisted.

flow.parent: A cotton fibre is about 2 to 3 cm long. The lamp wick has almost no twist, so its fibres slide apart easily.
flow.context: This step of Take a Thread Apart opens one ply into single fibres and measures how short a cotton fibre is.

flow.do: 1. Hold one end of the wool. Ask your child to twist the other end 40 times in one direction. 2. Keep it tight. Pinch the middle, and bring the two ends together. 3. Let go of the middle. 4. Watch the two halves wrap round each other.
flow.say: Twist the wool 40 times and keep it tight. Now fold it in half and let the middle go. Which way do the two halves wrap?
flow.kid: Twist the wool 40 times. Keep it tight. Fold it in half. Let the middle go. Watch.

check.q: Why are the plies of a thread twisted together the opposite way to their own twist?
options: To make the thread look pretty
So the two twists balance and the thread stays still
So the thread can stretch
check.why: A single twisted yarn tries to untwist. When two are twisted together the opposite way, each twist holds the other. The thread neither untwists nor curls.

flow.context: This is the last step of Take a Thread Apart. Here you twist a yarn, fold it and watch it turn into a two-ply cord by itself.

activities.title: Paper Ikat: colour the threads before you weave
activities.context: In this activity you draw a shape across loose paper strips and then weave them into a mat. You see what ikat weavers must plan for: the pattern is put on the threads before there is any cloth.

materials.item: white paper, A4 size
coloured paper or newspaper
sketch pens in two colours
scissors, a ruler and sticky tape

activities.record: Keep the woven mat. Beside it, write one sentence about what happened to your shape when you wove the strips.

setup.art: Eight white paper strips taped side by side at the top to a table, with a large blue diamond drawn across all of them.
setup.caption: 1. Tape 8 strips side by side. Draw one big shape across them all.

setup.art: Coloured paper strips woven over and under the white strips, so the blue diamond shows only in small squares.
setup.caption: 2. Weave coloured strips over and under. Look at your shape now.

setup.art: The same mat with every second white strip slid down a little, so the edge of the diamond looks stepped and feathered.
setup.caption: 3. Slide every second strip down a little. The edges turn feathery.

flow.do: 1. Cut 8 white strips, each 2 cm wide and 20 cm long. These are the warp. 2. Lay them side by side, touching, and tape their top ends to the table. 3. Draw one big, simple shape across all 8 strips, such as a diamond or a fish. Colour it in.
flow.say: These strips are our warp threads. Draw one big shape right across all of them. An ikat dyer does this with dye, before any weaving.
flow.kid: Cut 8 white strips. Tape them side by side. Draw one big shape across all of them. Colour it in.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper Ikat. Here you draw a shape across loose paper strips, as an ikat dyer colours loose threads.

flow.do: 1. Cut 8 coloured strips of the same size. These are the weft. 2. Weave the first one over, under, over, under across the white strips. 3. Weave the next one under, over, under, over. 4. Push each strip up close to the last. Weave all 8.
flow.say: Weave the coloured strips across. Before you start, guess: what will your shape look like when the mat is finished? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first: what will your shape look like after weaving? Then weave 8 strips, over and under.

ask.q: What happened to your shape?
good: Half of it is hidden under the coloured strips.
It shows only in small squares, where the white strip is on top.

flow.context: This step of Paper Ikat weaves plain strips across the drawn strips, to see what weaving does to the shape.

flow.do: 1. Slide every second white strip down by half a centimetre. 2. Look at the edges of the shape. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Real threads slip a little on the loom, as these strips just did. What has happened to the edge of your shape?
flow.kid: Slide every second white strip down a little. Look at the edge of your shape. What changed?

ask.q: In patola from Patan, the weft threads are dyed with the pattern too. What must the weaver get right?
good: Each weft colour must land exactly on the same colour in the warp.
Both sets of threads must be measured and dyed very exactly.

check.q: Why do ikat patterns have soft, feathered edges?
options: The dye is watery
The dyed threads shift a little when they are woven
The weaver draws the edges with a brush
check.why: In ikat the threads are dyed before weaving. On the loom each thread sits a little higher or lower than the one beside it, so the edge of each shape is stepped. A printed pattern has sharp edges, because it is put on after weaving.

flow.context: This is the last step of Paper Ikat. Here you shift some strips to see why ikat patterns have feathered edges.

activities.title: Label Hunt: what are our clothes made of?
activities.context: In this activity you read the labels inside ten clothes and bags at home. You count how many are made of natural fibres, synthetic fibres or blends, and ask why each fibre was chosen.

materials.item: clothes, bags and household cloth with labels, such as a school shirt, a sports T-shirt, a sweater, a sari, a bedsheet, a towel, socks and a school bag
paper and a pen

activities.record: Make a table with four columns: the thing, what the label says, natural or synthetic or blend, and why you think that fibre was chosen.

setup.art: A child turning the collar of a school shirt to read a small white label that says '65% polyester 35% cotton'.
setup.caption: 1. Find the label inside each thing and read the fibres.

setup.art: A page with a tally table: cotton only, polyester only, blend, other, with tally marks in each row.
setup.caption: 2. Tally the fibres. Which kind does your home have most of?

flow.do: 1. Find the label inside each thing. Look in the collar, in a side seam or inside a pocket. 2. Read the fibres and the percentages aloud. 3. Write them in the table.
flow.say: Every label names the fibres and how much of each. Read me this one. Which fibre is there most of?
flow.kid: Find the label in each thing. Read the fibres. Write them in your table.
flow.parent: Handloom saris, towels and older clothes often have no label. Write 'no label', and guess the fibre from how it feels.
flow.context: This is the first step of Label Hunt. Here you read the fibre labels inside ten things at home.

flow.do: 1. Mark each thing as natural, synthetic or blend. 2. Count each group. 3. Say which group is biggest.
flow.say: Cotton, wool, silk, jute and linen are natural. Polyester, nylon, acrylic and elastane are synthetic. Which group is biggest in our home?
flow.kid: Mark each thing: natural, synthetic or blend. Count each group. Which is biggest?
flow.parent: Viscose and rayon are made in a factory from plant cellulose. Put them in a fourth group, 'made from plants in a factory', or call them a blend of the two ideas.
flow.context: This step of Label Hunt sorts the ten things into natural fibres, synthetic fibres and blends, and counts each group.

flow.do: 1. Pick three things from the table. 2. For each, ask why that fibre suits that job. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Why is the school bag made of nylon or polyester? Why is the kitchen towel cotton? What would you wear beside a hot stove?
flow.kid: Pick three things. Why was each fibre chosen for its job? Say your reasons.

ask.q: Why is a towel made of cotton and a raincoat of polyester or nylon?
good: Cotton takes in water, so it dries the body.
Polyester and nylon take in very little water, so rain stays outside.

check.q: A label says '60% cotton, 40% polyester'. What kind of cloth is it?
options: A natural cloth
A synthetic cloth
A blend of natural and synthetic fibres
check.why: The yarn mixes two fibres, so the cloth is a blend. The cotton takes in sweat, and the polyester adds strength and dries fast.

flow.context: This is the last step of Label Hunt. Here you work out why each fibre was chosen for its job.

activities.title: One Cocoon, One Thread: a model of silk reeling
activities.context: In this activity you put the four stages of a silk moth's life in order. Then you wind two thread 'cocoons' round groundnuts and unwind them in two ways, to see why most silk makers do not let the moth come out.

materials.item: groundnuts in their shells, or two small erasers
sewing thread
small pieces of paper
scissors and a pen

activities.safety: A grown-up does the snipping in step 2.
activities.record: Draw the life of the silk moth as a circle with four stages and arrows. Under it, write how many pieces of thread each model cocoon gave.

setup.art: Four small paper cards in a circle joined by arrows, labelled egg, caterpillar, pupa in a cocoon and moth.
setup.caption: 1. Write the four stages on cards. Put them in order in a circle.

setup.art: Two groundnuts wound round and round with white thread, like small cocoons.
setup.caption: 2. Wind 3 metres of thread round each groundnut.

setup.art: One wound groundnut being unwound into a single long thread, and the other with a snipped hole at one end, giving many short pieces.
setup.caption: 3. Unwind one whole. Snip a hole in the other, then unwind it.

flow.do: 1. Write one stage on each piece of paper: egg, caterpillar, pupa in a cocoon, moth. 2. Mix them up. 3. Ask your child to lay them in order in a circle, and to say what happens at each stage.
flow.say: Put the four stages in order. Why is it a circle and not a line?
flow.kid: Put the four cards in order, in a circle. Say what happens at each stage.

ask.q: Why is the life of a moth drawn as a circle?
good: The moth lays eggs, and the eggs begin the same life again.

flow.context: This is the first step of One Cocoon, One Thread. Here you put the four stages of a silk moth's life in order.

flow.do: 1. Wind 3 metres of thread round each groundnut, crossing the turns in a figure of eight. Tuck in the end. 2. On the first, find the end and unwind it without breaking the thread. 3. On the second, a grown-up snips a small hole through the turns at one end. 4. Unwind the second one and count the pieces.
flow.say: A caterpillar winds one unbroken filament round their own body. Unwind the first cocoon whole. The second has a hole, as if the moth had come out. Count its pieces.
flow.kid: Wind thread round both groundnuts. Unwind the first in one piece. A grown-up snips a hole in the second. Unwind it and count the pieces.
flow.parent: A real moth does not cut the silk. She or he wets it with a liquid and pushes through, and that breaks the one filament into many short lengths.
flow.context: This step of One Cocoon, One Thread unwinds two model cocoons: one whole, and one with a hole like the hole a moth leaves.

flow.do: 1. Lay the long thread beside the short pieces. 2. Explain that long filament is unwound and used as it is, and short pieces must be spun like cotton. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Most silk makers heat the cocoons before the moths come out. Now you can see why. What do you think about that?
flow.kid: Look at the long thread and the short pieces. Why do silk makers stop the moth coming out? What do you think about it?

ask.q: Eri silk is made after the moths have left. What must be done with the broken cocoons?
good: The short pieces are spun into yarn, like cotton.
They cannot be unwound as one thread.

check.q: Why are most silk cocoons heated before the moth comes out?
options: To make the silk white
To keep the filament in one unbroken length
To help the moth grow
check.why: A moth that comes out breaks the filament into short pieces. Heating kills the pupa, so the cocoon can be unwound as one long filament. This is why some people choose eri silk or no silk.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Cocoon, One Thread. Here you compare the whole thread with the broken pieces and talk about how silk is made.

activities.title: Stitch Sampler: running stitch, backstitch and a kantha row
activities.context: In this activity you learn two hand stitches on two layers of old cloth, and stitch a few rows the way kantha quilts are made. Then you test what happens when the thread is cut. You need these stitches for the Leaky Seam Test.

materials.item: old cotton cloth, cut into squares about 15 cm by 15 cm
a sewing needle with a large eye
thread in a colour that shows on the cloth
a ruler, a ball pen and scissors
a bar of soap to hold the needle

activities.safety: A needle is sharp. Sit at a table to sew, and push the needle away from your other hand. Stick the needle in the bar of soap whenever it is not in use. Never hold a needle in your mouth.
activities.record: Keep the sampler. Label the three lines: running stitch, backstitch and kantha rows.

setup.art: Two squares of old cloth laid one on the other, with three pen lines and dots drawn across the top one.
setup.caption: 1. Lay one square on the other. Draw three lines with dots half a cm apart.

setup.art: A hand sewing a dashed line of running stitch along the first line, the needle halfway through the cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Line 1: running stitch. Down at one dot, up at the next.

setup.art: A close view of backstitch: the needle going back into the end of the last stitch, with arrows showing back, then forward.
setup.caption: 3. Line 2: backstitch. Go back one dot, then come up two dots ahead.

setup.art: The back of the sampler showing a dashed line under the running stitch and a thick overlapping line under the backstitch.
setup.caption: 4. Turn the cloth over and compare the backs.

flow.do: 1. Say the needle rules together. 2. Lay one square on the other. Draw three lines across the top square, each 12 cm long and 4 cm apart. 3. Mark a dot every half centimetre along each line. 4. Thread the needle, double the thread and knot the end.
flow.say: The needle lives in the soap when it is not in your hand. Now thread it, double the thread and tie a knot at the end.
flow.kid: Say the needle rules. Draw three lines with dots. Thread the needle and knot the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stitch Sampler. Here you learn the needle rules and mark two layers of cloth for three lines of stitches.

flow.do: 1. Line 1 is running stitch. Come up at the first dot, go down at the second, come up at the third, and so on. 2. Line 2 is backstitch. Come up at the second dot and go back down at the first. 3. Come up at the third dot and go back down at the second. Carry on to the end. 4. Finish each line with two small stitches on one spot.
flow.say: In running stitch the needle always goes forward. In backstitch it goes back one dot on top, then forward two dots underneath.
flow.kid: Sew line 1 in running stitch. Sew line 2 in backstitch: back one dot, forward two underneath.
flow.parent: Backstitch feels odd at first. Say 'back one, forward two' aloud with each stitch.
flow.context: This step of Stitch Sampler sews one line of running stitch and one line of backstitch through two layers of cloth.

flow.do: 1. On line 3, sew a row of running stitch. 2. Sew two more rows beside it, half a centimetre apart. 3. Pull each thread a little, so the cloth ripples. 4. Turn the sampler over and compare the backs of all three lines.
flow.say: Kantha quilts from Bengal are made like this: rows and rows of running stitch through layers of old saris. Feel how the layers have become one cloth.
flow.kid: Sew three rows of running stitch close together. Pull the thread a little. Feel the ripples. Turn the cloth over.

ask.q: How do the backs of the running stitch and the backstitch differ?
good: The running stitch looks the same on both sides: a dashed line.
The backstitch has a thicker, overlapping line on the back, so it used more thread.

flow.context: This step of Stitch Sampler sews rows of running stitch close together, the way layers of old cloth are joined in a kantha quilt.

flow.do: 1. Pull the two layers gently apart beside line 1, then beside line 2. Look between the stitches. 2. On line 1, snip off the knot at the start and the two small stitches at the end. Pull the thread from one end. 3. Do the same on line 2.
flow.say: Pull the layers apart at each line. Which line opens more? Now I cut both ends of each thread free. Pull the thread. What happens?
flow.kid: Pull the layers apart at each line. Which opens more? A grown-up cuts the thread ends free. Pull each thread.

check.q: The two ends of a running stitch thread are cut free and one end is pulled. What happens?
options: Nothing: the stitches hold
The whole thread slides out and the seam opens
Only the first stitch comes out
check.why: A running stitch thread passes straight through the cloth, in and out. With no knot to stop it, the whole thread can be drawn out. A backstitch loops back on itself, so it grips and comes out only stitch by stitch.

flow.context: This is the last step of Stitch Sampler. Here you test the two stitches by pulling the layers apart and by cutting the thread ends free.

activities.title: Old Cloth, New Job: a cupboard check and an interview
activities.context: In this activity you find five cloth things at home that nobody uses any more. You work out how each was made, choose a next job for it, and ask an older person what their family did with old cloth.

materials.item: cloth things that nobody uses, such as an outgrown T-shirt, a torn bedsheet, a single sock, an old dupatta and a faded towel
paper and a pen

activities.record: Make a table with five columns: the thing, its fibre, woven or knitted, what is wrong with it, and its next job.

setup.art: A small heap on a bed: an outgrown T-shirt, a torn bedsheet, one sock, a faded towel and an old dupatta.
setup.caption: 1. Collect five cloth things that nobody uses.

setup.art: A child pulling a T-shirt sideways with one hand and reading its label with the other, a table half filled in beside her.
setup.caption: 2. For each one, find the fibre and whether it is woven or knitted.

setup.art: A child with a notebook sitting beside her grandmother, who is holding up a patchwork quilt.
setup.caption: 3. Ask an older person what their family did with old cloth.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the five things. 2. For each one, read the label for the fibre. 3. Pull it gently and look closely, to decide whether it is woven or knitted. 4. Write what is wrong with it: too small, torn, faded or thin. 5. Choose its next job: mend, pass on, remake, use as a rag, or give for recycling.
flow.say: How was this one made, woven or knitted? Will its cut edge fray? What could it become, now that you know that?
flow.kid: Look at each thing. Is it woven or knitted? What is wrong with it? Choose its next job.

ask.q: Why is an old T-shirt good for cutting into strips, when an old bedsheet is not?
good: T-shirt cloth is knitted, so the cut edges curl and do not fray.
A woven bedsheet frays at every cut edge unless it is hemmed.

flow.parent: Good answers use how the cloth was made. A knitted wool sweater can be unravelled. A woven sheet can be cut and hemmed into handkerchiefs or bags. A cotton banian makes a soft duster.
flow.context: This is the first step of Old Cloth, New Job. Here you work out how five old cloth things were made, and choose a next job for each.

flow.do: 1. Sit with an older person, or phone one. 2. Ask the three questions below and write the answers. 3. Thank them.
flow.say: Let's ask a grown-up, or someone older, a few questions. When you were ten, what happened to old clothes in your home? Who mended them? Do you remember anything that was made from old cloth?
flow.kid: Ask an older person three questions about old clothes. Write the answers.
flow.parent: Listen for quilts, cradles made from old saris, pot holders, lamp wicks, dusters and clothes handed down. Many families exchanged old clothes for steel vessels.
flow.context: This step of Old Cloth, New Job is an interview with an older person about what their family did with old cloth.

flow.do: 1. Choose one of the five things and do its next job today, or plan the day for it. 2. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which one shall we do today? What do we need for it?
flow.kid: Choose one thing. Give it its next job today, or plan when you will.

check.q: Which use keeps the most of the work that went into a shirt?
options: Tearing it into fibre for new yarn
Passing it on for someone else to wear
Burning it for heat
check.why: A shirt that is worn again keeps its spinning, weaving, dyeing and stitching. Recycling into fibre keeps only the fibre, and shortens it. Burning keeps nothing.

flow.context: This is the last step of Old Cloth, New Job. Here you give one old thing its next job.

projects.title: The Chindi Coaster: weave old cloth on a card loom
projects.context: In this four-day project you make a small loom from a piece of carton. You wind a warp of string on it and weave strips of an old T-shirt across, the way chindi rugs are woven from scraps of cloth. You finish with a coaster for a tumbler.

materials.item: stiff cardboard from a carton, 12 cm wide and 14 cm tall
cotton string or thick thread for the warp
an old T-shirt or banian in one or two colours, to cut into strips
scissors, a ruler, a pen and sticky tape
a hair pin or a large safety pin, to carry the strip
a comb or a fork, to push the rows down
squared paper from a maths notebook

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the notches in the cardboard, which is tough to cut.

schedule.what: Cut 10 notches at the top and bottom of the card. Wind the string up and down to make 10 warp threads. Cut the T-shirt into strips.
Weave 8 rows of T-shirt strip, over and under, pushing each row down with the comb.
Plan a stripe or a pattern on squared paper. Weave 8 more rows.
Cut the coaster off the loom, knot the warp ends in pairs and try it under a tumbler.

projects.record: Keep the squared-paper plan and the coaster. Write how many warp threads, how many rows and how many crossings your coaster has.

setup.art: A piece of brown cardboard with 10 small notches along the top edge and 10 along the bottom, and white string wound up and down between them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 10 notches top and bottom. Wind the string to make 10 warp threads.

setup.art: A hair pin pulling a red strip of T-shirt cloth over and under the white strings.
setup.caption: 2. Weave a strip of old T-shirt over and under the warp.

setup.art: A comb pushing a new row down against the rows already woven.
setup.caption: 3. Push each row down with a comb.

setup.art: A finished small woven mat with knotted string ends, under a steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 4. Cut it off the loom, knot the ends and use it.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts 10 notches, each 1 cm deep and 1 cm apart, along the top edge of the card. Start 1.5 cm from the side. Cut 10 more along the bottom edge. 2. Tape one end of the string to the back. Bring it through the first bottom notch and up the front to the first top notch. 3. Take it behind the card to the second top notch and down the front to the second bottom notch. 4. Carry on until 10 strings cross the front. Tape the end at the back. 5. Cut rings 1.5 cm wide from the body of the T-shirt. Cut each ring open to make a long strip.
flow.say: This string is the warp. It must be tight, like the strings of a veena. How many warp threads can you count on the front?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the notches. Wind the string up and down the front. Count 10 warp threads. Cut the T-shirt into strips.
flow.parent: Pull each T-shirt strip gently and its edges curl in, so it becomes a soft round yarn. T-shirt cloth is knitted, so the cut edges do not fray.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Chindi Coaster. Here you make a card loom, wind the warp and cut an old T-shirt into strips for the weft.

flow.do: 1. Fix one end of a strip in the hair pin. 2. Weave the first row: over one string, under the next, right across. Leave a tail of 3 cm at the start. 3. Weave back the other way: under where the last row went over. 4. Push each row down with the comb. 5. Do not pull the strip tight at the edges. 6. To join a new strip, lay its end over the old end for 3 cm and weave them together. 7. Weave 8 rows.
flow.say: Weave the strip over one string, then under the next, and keep going. On the way back, do the opposite. Go under the strings that you went over. What would happen if two rows went the same way?
flow.kid: Weave over one string and under the next. Go back the opposite way. Push each row down. Weave 8 rows.

ask.q: What would happen if two rows went over and under the same strings?
good: They would slide together into one thick row.
They would not lock each other, so the cloth would be loose there.

flow.parent: If the edges are pulled tight, the coaster grows narrow in the middle. Leave a small loop of strip at each turn.
flow.context: This step of the Chindi Coaster weaves the first 8 rows of old T-shirt strip across the warp.

flow.do: 1. On squared paper, draw a grid 10 squares wide and 16 squares tall. 2. Colour a square wherever the weft goes over a warp thread. Rows 1 to 8 are done already. 3. Plan rows 9 to 16: change the colour of the strip to make stripes, or try going over two and under two. 4. Weave rows 9 to 16 from the plan.
flow.say: A weaver plans on squared paper before touching the loom. Each square is one crossing. Colour the squares where your strip will be on top.
flow.kid: Draw a grid 10 wide and 16 tall. Colour where the strip goes over. Plan 8 more rows. Weave them.
flow.parent: Over two and under two makes a looser, softer band. If each row steps one string sideways, slanting lines appear, as in denim.
flow.context: This step of the Chindi Coaster plans a pattern on squared paper and weaves 8 more rows from the plan.

flow.do: 1. Turn the loom over. Cut the strings across the middle of the back. 2. Lift the weaving off the card. 3. At each end, knot the strings together in pairs, close to the weaving. 4. Trim the ends. 5. Count the crossings: warp threads times rows. 6. Stand a tumbler on the coaster.
flow.say: Before I cut the strings, tell me: what holds your coaster together? What will the knots at the ends do?
flow.kid: Cut the strings at the back. Lift the weaving off. Knot the strings in pairs. Count the crossings.

check.q: Why must the warp ends of the coaster be knotted after it is cut off the loom?
options: To make it look pretty
So the end rows cannot slide off the warp
To make the coaster stretch
check.why: Woven cloth is held only by friction at the crossings. At a cut end, the last row has nothing beyond it and can slide off. That is what happened to the straight cut edge in the Fray Test. A knot blocks the way.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Chindi Coaster. Here you cut the weaving off the loom, knot the warp ends and count the crossings.

challenges.title: The No-Leak Seam: hold the mustard seeds with the least sewing
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Leaky Seam Test, the shortest stitches held the mustard seeds but took the longest to sew. Here you design a seam that holds the seeds and takes less time or less thread.
challenges.problem: Sew a seam 8 cm long that joins two pieces of cloth. In the tumbler test, with 20 rubs, it must let through no more than 2 mustard seeds. Among seams that pass, the best one takes the least time to sew.
constraints: Use the same cloth, the same thread and the same 8 cm line as in the Leaky Seam Test.
Test it exactly as before: stretch the seam over the tumbler and rub 1 level teaspoon of mustard seeds across it 20 times.
Time the sewing from the first stitch to the last knot.
Measure the thread before you start and after you finish, to find how much you used.
materials: old cotton cloth cut into pieces 10 cm by 8 cm
a needle with a large eye, thread, scissors and a bar of soap
the steel tumbler, rubber band and plate from the Leaky Seam Test
a ruler and a phone timer
general: Sew a backstitch with stitches half a centimetre long.
Sew two rows of running stitch side by side, with the stitches of one row beside the gaps of the other.
Sew a running stitch with stitches a quarter of a centimetre long, as in seam C.
creative: Fold the two flaps over together and sew them down a second time, like the thick seam on the side of jeans.
Sew a running stitch with one backstitch after every third stitch.
Sew over and over the two edges, so the thread wraps round them like a spring.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own seam. Draw it from the side, sew it, time it and test it. Did it pass? Was it faster than seam C in the Leaky Seam Test?

setup.art: Two small cloth pieces being sewn together with two rows of stitches, a phone timer running beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Sew your seam design. Time it.

setup.art: The seam stretched over a steel tumbler with mustard seeds on top and a finger rubbing them across.
setup.caption: 2. Test it with mustard seeds, 20 rubs.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table from the Leaky Seam Test. 2. Write down the minutes that seam C took and the seeds it let through. 3. Those are the numbers to beat.
flow.say: Seam C held the seeds but was slow. Why was it slow? What else could close the gaps between stitches?
flow.kid: Find the time for seam C in your table. That is the time to beat. How else could you close the gaps?
flow.context: This is the first step of the No-Leak Seam challenge. Here you find the time to beat from the Leaky Seam Test.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual ideas. 2. Choose one and sew it, with the timer running. 3. Test it with the mustard seeds. 4. Write the time, the thread used and the seeds that fell through.
flow.say: Which idea will you try first? Why do you think it will close the gaps?
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Sew it and time it. Test it with the seeds. Write the numbers.
flow.context: This step of the No-Leak Seam challenge sews and tests one seam design.

flow.do: 1. Design a seam of your own and draw it from the side. 2. Sew it, time it and test it. 3. Compare all your seams in one table.
flow.say: Which seam passed the test in the least time? What made it work?
flow.kid: Design your own seam. Draw it. Sew it and test it. Which seam is best?

check.q: Why does a second row of running stitch, set beside the gaps of the first, stop more seeds?
options: Two threads are heavier than one
Each gap in one row is pinned shut by a stitch in the other
The seeds stick to the thread
check.why: A running stitch leaves the cloth free to open between its needle holes. A second row with its holes beside those gaps pins the cloth where the first row left it free.

flow.context: This is the last step of the No-Leak Seam challenge. Here you design your own seam and compare it with the others.

challenges.title: Wear It Uncut: dress in one cloth with no scissors and no pins
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A sari, a veshti, a mundu and a dhoti are worn just as they come off the loom, so no cloth is cut away and wasted. Here you design a way to wear one uncut cloth so that it stays on while you move.
challenges.problem: Use one uncut rectangle of cloth to dress yourself over your ordinary clothes. The cloth must stay on through 10 jumps and a walk across the room, with both hands free.
constraints: Use one cloth only, and do not cut it.
No pins, clips, rubber bands or belts. Use only folds, pleats, tucks, rolls and knots.
You must be able to walk, sit down and lift both arms.
Wear it over your ordinary clothes, so you can test it without worry.
materials: a dupatta, a thorthu or thin towel, or a small bedsheet
a clear floor to jump on
general: Wrap the cloth round the waist and roll the top edge over itself twice, as a lungi or mundu is worn.
Fold part of the cloth into pleats and tuck the pleats in at the waist, as in a sari or a veshti.
Knot two corners together over one shoulder.
creative: Pass one end between the legs and tuck it in at the back, as a dhoti is worn for work.
Twist one end of the cloth into a rope and use it as the belt for the rest.
Cross two corners over the chest and knot them behind the neck.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to wear the cloth. Test it with 10 jumps and a walk across the room. Draw it, and write what holds it up.

setup.art: A child wrapping a striped towel round her waist over her clothes and rolling its top edge down.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap, pleat, tuck, roll or knot one uncut cloth.

setup.art: The same child jumping with both hands in the air while the wrapped cloth stays in place.
setup.caption: 2. Test it: 10 jumps and a walk, hands free.

flow.do: 1. Clear the floor. 2. Wrap the cloth round the waist and roll the top edge over twice. 3. Jump 10 times and walk across the room. 4. Count the jumps before the cloth slips.
flow.say: Start with the simplest way: wrap and roll. How many jumps does it last? What is holding it up?
flow.kid: Wrap the cloth round your waist. Roll the top edge over twice. Jump 10 times. Does it stay?

ask.q: What holds a rolled waist in place?
good: Friction between the layers of cloth pressed together.
The roll squeezes the layers tight round the body.

flow.context: This is the first step of Wear It Uncut. Here you try the simplest way of wearing an uncut cloth, and test it by jumping.

flow.do: 1. Try pleats: fold part of the cloth back and forth five times and tuck the pleats in at the waist. 2. Try a knot over one shoulder. 3. Test each with 10 jumps. 4. Write which lasted longest.
flow.say: Pleats put many layers of cloth in one place. Does that hold better or worse than the roll? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Try pleats tucked in at the waist. Try a knot over one shoulder. Test each with 10 jumps.
flow.parent: Pleats hold well because many layers press on each other, so friction is high. They also leave room for the legs to move.
flow.context: This step of Wear It Uncut tests pleats and knots, the usual ways of holding an uncut cloth in place.

flow.do: 1. Design your own way. 2. Test it with 10 jumps, a walk, sitting down and lifting both arms. 3. Draw it and label what holds it up.
flow.say: Now invent your own. What will hold it up when you jump? Draw it and mark the place where friction or a knot does the work.
flow.kid: Invent your own way. Test it: jump, walk, sit and lift your arms. Draw it.

check.q: Why does a sari waste no cloth, when a shirt cut from the same cloth does?
options: A sari is made of better cloth
A sari is worn as one whole rectangle, with nothing cut away
A sari is smaller than a shirt
check.why: A shirt is made of curved pieces cut out of a rectangle, so scraps are left between the pieces. A sari is worn as it comes off the loom, shaped by pleats and tucks, so nothing is cut away.

flow.context: This is the last step of Wear It Uncut. Here you design and test your own way of wearing one uncut cloth.

items.p: What is weaving?
opts: Crossing two sets of threads, over and under
items.why: Weaving crosses warp threads and weft threads at right angles. Twisting fibres is spinning, and pulling one thread into loops is knitting. Choosing one of those means the three words need another look.

items.p: The threads that run along the length of a woven cloth are called the ____.
items.why: The warp is stretched tight on the loom first. The weft is then woven across it.

items.p: True or false: a T-shirt is woven.
items.why: False. A T-shirt is knitted from one thread in rows of loops. A strong answer says how to check: the cloth stretches, and a close look shows loops, not crossing threads.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words are used all through the unit. A strong answer can point to each one on a real shirt.
pairs: pulling one yarn into rows of loops
the side edge where the weft turns back
a line of stitches joining two pieces

items.p: Sort these fibres by where they come from.
items.a: see items
items.why: Cotton, jute and coir are plant fibres. Wool, silk and pashmina are animal fibres. Nylon and polyester are made in factories, mostly from petroleum.

items.p: Remember Woven or Knitted, where a bottle hung from strips of cloth. Explain why the knitted strip stretched more.
items.a: The thread in knitted cloth runs in loops, so each row holds much more thread than the cloth is wide. When the bottle pulled, the loops opened out and the strip grew longer. The woven thread was already nearly straight, so it had no length to spare.
items.why: A strong answer uses the thread lengths: the knitted thread was 3 or 4 times as long as its cloth was wide, and the woven thread was only a little longer.

items.p: Put the stages of a silk moth's life in order. Start with the egg.
items.why: The egg hatches into a caterpillar. The caterpillar spins a cocoon and becomes a pupa inside. The pupa becomes a moth, who lays eggs.

items.p: Draw the path of one thread in a woven cloth and in a knitted cloth, side by side.
items.a: The woven thread goes straight across, over one thread and under the next. The knitted thread goes up and down in a row of loops.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the woven thread almost straight and the knitted thread looping, so it is clear which has spare length.

items.p: Which bird stitches the edges of a leaf together to hold a nest?
items.why: The tailorbird pierces the leaf edges and pulls plant fibre or spider silk through. The baya weaver weaves a hanging nest from strips of grass.

items.p: Three of these are natural fibres. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Cotton and jute come from plants, and wool from sheep. Polyester is made in a factory from petroleum.

items.p: True or false: twisting short fibres together makes a yarn that can hold a load.
items.why: True. The twist presses the fibres together, and friction stops them sliding apart. A lamp wick with little twist pulls apart easily.

items.p: Label a drawing of a card loom: warp, weft, notch and comb.
a: Warp: the strings running up and down
Notch: the cut that holds a warp string
items.why: The warp is held tight by the notches. The weft goes over and under it, and the comb packs the rows together.
items.art: A card loom with strings, a half-woven strip and a comb, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Two people talk about an outgrown school shirt in good condition.
items.a: A strong answer sees that passing the shirt on keeps all the spinning, weaving and stitching, while recycling keeps only the fibre and shortens it. It agrees with one person and says when the other is right: a shirt too torn to wear is better recycled than thrown away.
items.why: Both uses are better than the dustbin. The order matters: wear again first, recycle last.

views.says: Give it for recycling. A factory can turn it into new fibre.
Pass it on to a younger child. It is still a good shirt.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with? Use what you know about what recycling does to fibres. Then say when the other person would be right.

items.p: In a running stitch, the needle goes:
opts: down and up along a line
items.why: A running stitch goes down and up along a line and leaves a dashed line of thread. Going back each time makes a backstitch.

items.p: Why does the cut edge of a bedsheet need a hem? Use the word 'fray'.
items.a: A cut edge of woven cloth will fray, because the threads along the edge have nothing outside them to hold them in. A hem folds the cut edge inside and stitches it down, so the threads cannot slide out.
items.why: A strong answer says what fraying is and how the fold stops it, as in the Fray Test.

items.p: One row of thread pulled from 5 cm of T-shirt cloth is 18 cm long. What does this show?
opts: The thread is made of rubber
Cotton grows when it is cut
items.why: The thread is more than 3 times as long as the cloth is wide, so it must be folded into loops. That spare length is where the stretch comes from.

items.p: In the Leaky Seam Test, the longest stitches leaked most. Explain why, using the words 'needle holes' and 'gap'.
items.a: A running stitch pins the two cloths together only at the needle holes. Between the holes the cloths can pull apart and leave a gap. When the holes are 1 cm apart the gap is wide enough for a mustard seed. Short stitches leave only small gaps.
items.why: A strong answer links the length of the stitch to the size of the gap, and the size of the gap to the size of the seed.

items.p: True or false: cloth cut on the slant frays more than cloth cut straight along the threads.
items.why: False. On a slant cut no thread runs along the edge, so no whole thread can slide off. A straight cut frays most.

items.p: A pattern made by tying and dyeing the threads before weaving is called ____.
items.why: In ikat the pattern is dyed into the threads first. It appears, with feathered edges, as the cloth is woven.

items.p: Sort these cloths by how the pattern is made.
items.a: see items
items.why: Kanchipuram borders, jamdani and Paithani patterns are made on the loom with coloured threads. Bandhani and Pochampally ikat are tied and dyed. Kantha, Toda embroidery and kasuti are stitched with a needle.

items.p: Which is the safest to wear beside a gas stove?
items.why: Synthetic fibres melt near a flame and stick to the skin. Cotton can burn, but it does not melt and stick.

items.p: Draw a seam with long running stitches, pulled open. Mark the place where a seed could pass.
items.a: Two cloths pulled apart with thread crossing between them like the rungs of a ladder. The gaps between the rungs are marked.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the cloth pinned only at the needle holes and open between them.
items.art: Two blank cloth edges facing each other.

items.p: Three people talk about silk.
items.a: A strong answer uses the facts: a moth who comes out breaks the filament, so reeled silk needs the pupa to die. Eri silk lets the moth out but is less shiny and costs more. It picks one view, gives a reason, and answers one point from another view fairly.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about how to treat other animals. No answer is the only right one.

views.says: Unbroken filament gives the strongest, shiniest silk, and my family lives by it.
I wait until the moths have left. The silk is duller, but no pupa is killed for it.

views.who: A person who wears no silk
views.says: The moths on a silk farm cannot fly or feed. I would rather wear cotton.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Give your reason. Then answer one point made by another person.

items.p: Put these steps in order, from the cotton field to a finished shirt.
a: Weave or knit the yarn into cloth
Cut the cloth and stitch the pieces
items.why: Fibre comes first, then yarn, then cloth, then the garment. Dyeing can happen to the yarn or to the cloth.
items: Weave or knit the yarn into cloth
Cut the cloth and stitch the pieces

items.p: A male baya weaver has no hands. Describe how he starts a nest and what he builds it from.
items.a: He tears long strips from paddy, grass or palm leaves with his beak. He knots the first strips round a thin twig. Then he weaves more strips in and out with his beak, holding them with his feet.
items.why: A strong answer names the material, the first knot and the weaving, and says that the beak does the work.

items.p: Match each fibre to a job it suits.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each fibre is chosen for what it does: jute is strong and cheap, wool traps air, cotton takes in water, coir stands up to water, and nylon keeps water out.
pairs: a school bag for rainy days

items.p: Why is denim blue outside and pale inside?
opts: The inside is washed more often
The blue threads lie mostly on the outside
The inside is a different cloth
items.why: Denim is a twill. Its blue warp threads pass over three white weft threads and under one, so the outside shows mostly blue and the inside mostly white.

items.p: Three of these are knitted. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A sari is woven on a loom from warp and weft. T-shirts, socks and sweaters are knitted from one thread in loops.

items.p: Label a drawing of a hem seen from the side: the fold, the hidden cut edge and the stitches.
a: The stitches that hold the fold down
items.why: A hem works because the cut edge is shut inside the fold, where its threads cannot slide out.
items.art: A side view of a cloth edge folded over twice, with three blank label lines.

items.p: A sock has a ladder running down it. Explain how one broken loop caused it.
items.a: In knitted cloth each loop is held by the loop next to it in the column. When one loop breaks, the next loop has nothing to hold it and slips out, and then the one after that. The line of slipped loops is the ladder.
items.why: A strong answer says that every loop depends on another loop, which is the cost of knitting with one thread.

items.p: Cloth rots in the ground. Explain how a lump of fired clay can show that people wove 26,000 years ago.
items.a: Wet clay was pressed against woven cloth and took its print. The clay was then baked in a fire and became hard. The cloth rotted, but the print of crossing threads stayed in the clay, and the clay can be dated.
items.why: A strong answer separates the cloth, which is gone, from the evidence, which is its print.

items.p: Three people talk about handloom cloth.
items.a: A strong answer uses facts from the unit: a handloom is slow, needs no electricity and can weave patterns machines weave badly, and about 35 lakh people work in handloom. Mill cloth is cheap enough for everyone. It picks a side and gives one fair point from another side.
items.why: This is a real trade-off between price, skill and people's work. There is no single right answer.

views.says: My skill took years to learn. If nobody pays for it, it will be lost.
I need three uniforms for two children. I must buy the cheapest cloth.
My looms make cheap cloth for lakhs of people, and they give work too.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most, and why? Then say one thing that another person has right.

items.p: A thread is pulled out of woven cloth 10 cm wide. About how long is the thread?
items.why: A woven thread bends only slightly over and under the others, so it is just a little longer than the cloth is wide. A knitted thread would be about 30 cm.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a tight knit stretch less than a loose knit? Say what stays the same.
items.a: Cut a strip of the same size from a tight knit and a loose knit of the same fibre, both cut across the rows. Mark 20 cm on each, hang the same bottle for 10 seconds and measure. Keep the same width, direction, fibre, bottle and time. Change only how tight the knit is.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing and names at least three things kept the same.

items.p: True or false: yarn spun from torn-up old clothes is as strong as yarn spun from new fibre.
items.why: False. Tearing cloth back into fibre shortens the fibres. Short fibres overlap less, so the recycled yarn is weaker.

items.p: The body louse lives only in clothing. What can their DNA help scientists find out?
opts: What colour the first clothes were
Roughly when people began to wear clothes
items.why: Body lice could not exist before clothes. Their DNA shows when they split from head lice, at least 83,000 years ago, so clothes are at least that old.

items.p: Someone says natural fibres are always better for the Earth. Give one piece of evidence for and one against.
items.a: For: cotton, wool and jute rot back into soil, while polyester lasts for centuries and sheds plastic microfibres. Against: growing cotton takes a great deal of water, hundreds to thousands of litres for one T-shirt by different estimates, and often much pesticide.
items.why: A strong answer gives real evidence on both sides before deciding.

items.p: A ____ loom is driven by a motor, and a handloom is worked by a person.
items.why: A power loom weaves many metres in the time a handloom weaves one, which is why mill cloth is cheaper.

items.p: Sort these old things by the best way to use their cloth again.
items.a: see items
items.why: Hand-knitted things are one yarn in loops, so they can be unravelled and knitted again. Woven things fray when cut, so they are cut to a new shape and hemmed.

items.p: Why do tailors use long running stitches to hold a blouse together for a first fitting?
opts: They are quick, and easy to pull out
items.why: Long running stitches are fast to sew, and the thread slides out easily afterwards. A strong seam is sewn later with small machine stitches.

items.p: Put these in order, from the oldest to the newest.
a: Prints of woven cloth in clay at Pavlov
Cotton thread in a copper bead at Mehrgarh
The Jacquard loom with punched cards
Nylon, an early fully synthetic fibre
items.why: The clay prints are about 26,000 years old and the Mehrgarh thread about 7,000 to 8,000. The Jacquard loom dates from 1804 and nylon from 1935.
items: The Jacquard loom with punched cards
Nylon, an early fully synthetic fibre
Prints of woven cloth in clay at Pavlov
Cotton thread in a copper bead at Mehrgarh

items.p: When a sweater is unravelled, all the wool is still there. Is the sweater still there? Give your reasons.
items.a: There is no single right answer. One good answer: the wool is there but the sweater is not, because a sweater is wool arranged in loops of a certain shape. Another: nothing has been lost, so the sweater is only waiting to be knitted again.
items.why: A strong answer says clearly what the child thinks a sweater is, the material or the arrangement, and gives a reason.

items.p: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each claim in this unit rests on something people found and measured. A strong answer can say why the evidence fits the claim.
pairs: Prints of crossing threads in fired clay
Cotton fibres inside a copper bead
cotton thread was used at Mehrgarh
clothes shed microfibres into the sea
A scrap of three-ply cord on a stone tool

items.p: In three of these, the pattern is made before or during weaving. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Chikankari is stitched on to finished cloth with a needle. Ikat threads are dyed before weaving, and jamdani and Kanchipuram borders are made on the loom.

items.p: Label a drawing of a finished baya nest: the knot on the twig, the egg chamber and the entrance tube.
a: The knot round the twig, at the top
The round egg chamber, in the middle
The long entrance tube, hanging down
items.why: The nest hangs from its first knot. The eggs lie in the round chamber, and the tube that hangs down makes it hard for a snake to get in.
items.art: A hanging grass nest shaped like a flask with a long neck pointing down, with three blank label lines.

quiz.p: In woven cloth, what does the weft thread do?
opts: It runs along the length, held tight
It runs across, over and under the warp
quiz.why: The weft runs across the cloth, over and under the warp threads. The warp is the set held tight along the length. If you chose loops, that is knitting.

quiz.p: Under a lens, a cloth shows columns of tiny V-shaped loops. How was it made?
quiz.why: Rows of loops mean knitting. Woven cloth shows two sets of threads crossing at right angles.

quiz.p: Why does knitted cotton stretch more than woven cotton?
opts: Its looped thread can open out
quiz.why: A knitted row holds 3 or 4 times as much thread as the cloth is wide, bent into loops. A pull opens the loops. The cotton itself is the same.

quiz.p: A cotton fibre is only 3 cm long. How can a cotton yarn be many metres long?
opts: The fibres are glued end to end
Twisted fibres overlap and grip each other
The fibres are tied in knots
quiz.why: Spinning overlaps the fibres and twists them. The twist presses them together, and friction stops them sliding apart. Nothing is glued or tied.

quiz.p: Which of these fibres comes from an animal?
quiz.why: Pashmina is the under-hair of a goat from Ladakh. Jute and linen come from plant stems, and polyester from a factory.

quiz.p: What is inside a silk cocoon just before the moth comes out?
quiz.why: The caterpillar spins the cocoon and becomes a pupa inside. The pupa then becomes the moth. The egg stage came much earlier.

quiz.p: Two seams join the same cloth, one with long stitches and one with short. Which lets more seeds through?
opts: Both let the same number through
quiz.why: The cloths are pinned together only at the needle holes. Long stitches leave long gaps between the holes, so more seeds pass.

quiz.p: True or false: the selvedge of a cloth frays faster than a cut edge.
quiz.why: False. At the selvedge the weft turns back into the cloth, so there are no cut ends to slide out. A cut edge frays.

quiz.p: In which of these is the pattern stitched on with a needle?
quiz.why: Kasuti is embroidery from Karnataka. Ikat and bandhani are tied and dyed, and ajrakh is printed with wooden blocks.

quiz.p: What does a tailorbird use to stitch a leaf?
opts: Strips of grass woven over and under
quiz.why: A tailorbird pierces the leaf edge and pulls fibre or spider silk through. Weaving strips of grass is the baya weaver's way.

quiz.p: An old cotton sari is too thin to wear. Which use keeps it as cloth?
opts: Stitching it into a kantha quilt
quiz.why: In a kantha quilt the layers of old sari are still cloth, joined by running stitch. Tearing it into fibre keeps only the fibre.

applications: Surgeons close wounds with stitches, and choose the stitch and the thread for each part of the body.
Tyres and conveyor belts have layers of strong cords and woven cloth inside the rubber, which carry the load.
Cloth woven from carbon fibre or glass fibre is set in resin to make light, strong parts for aircraft, rockets and cricket helmets.
Mats woven from coir or jute are laid on new slopes beside roads. They hold the soil until grass grows, and then rot away.
Doctors replace damaged blood vessels with tubes of woven or knitted polyester.
Parachutes and car airbags are tightly woven nylon, so that very little air passes through.
Sports clothes are knitted so that they stretch with the body, and many are made of polyester because it dries fast.

open_questions.q: How did weaving begin: with baskets, with nets or with mats?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest cloth has rotted away. Only a few prints in clay and scraps of cord are left, and they are too few to show what came first.

open_questions.q: How much harm do microfibres do to sea animals and to people?
open_questions.why_open: The fibres have been found in water, salt, fish and air. Measuring what they do inside a living body over many years is slow and difficult work.

open_questions.q: Can a cloth made of cotton and polyester together be turned back into good new yarn?
open_questions.why_open: The two fibres are twisted together in every thread. Ways to separate them exist in laboratories, but they are costly and are only now being tried in factories.

open_questions.q: How much of a baya's weaving is known from birth, and how much is learned?
open_questions.why_open: Young males weave badly and improve. Nobody has yet followed wild bayas closely enough to say how much comes from practice and how much from watching others.

open_questions.q: When did people first wear clothes?
open_questions.why_open: The DNA of body lice says at least 83,000 years ago and perhaps 170,000. No clothes that old have survived to check.

jokes.a: It always gets to the point.

jokes.j: What did the warp thread say to the weft thread?
jokes.a: Half the time you go right over my head.

jokes.j: Why did the T-shirt win the yoga prize?
jokes.a: Nobody else could stretch like that and spring back.

jokes.j: What did the hem say to the cut edge?
jokes.a: Don't fray. I've got you covered.

jokes.j: The caterpillar was asked to come out and play. What did they say?
What does one running stitch say to the next?
jokes.a: See you on the other side.

jokes.j: Why did the ikat thread finish its homework first?
jokes.a: It did all its colouring before the weaving began.

jokes.j: Why did the baya weaver say no to a loom?
jokes.a: His beak works even in a power cut.

jokes.j: Why did the short cotton fibre join the yarn?
jokes.a: It wanted to go a long way with its friends.

maths.problem: In Woven or Knitted, a woven strip stretched 0.3 cm. A knitted strip cut across the T-shirt stretched 9 cm. How many times as much did the knitted strip stretch?
maths.explain: 0.3 cm is 3 tenths of a centimetre, and 9 cm is 90 tenths. 90 divided by 3 is 30. So the knitted strip stretched 30 times as much as the woven strip.
maths.context: In Woven or Knitted you hang the same bottle of water from strips of woven and knitted cotton and measure the stretch. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Saying '30 times as much' shows how different the two cloths are far better than saying 'more'.

maths.problem: In Woven or Knitted, one row of thread pulled from 5 cm of T-shirt cloth was 18 cm long. The front of the T-shirt is 40 cm wide. About how long is the thread in one row across the front?
maths.explain: 40 cm is 8 times 5 cm. Each 5 cm of cloth holds 18 cm of thread. 8 times 18 is 144. So one row across the front holds about 144 cm of thread.
maths.context: In Woven or Knitted you pull one row of thread out of a small piece of T-shirt cloth and measure it. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A small measured piece lets us work out what a whole T-shirt holds, without unravelling the T-shirt.

maths.problem: One row across a T-shirt front holds about 144 cm of thread. The front is 60 cm long and has about 16 rows in every centimetre. About how many metres of thread are in the front?
maths.answer: About 1,380 metres, which is more than 1 kilometre.
maths.explain: First find the rows: 60 times 16 is 960 rows. Each row holds 144 cm. 960 times 144 is 138,240 cm. Divide by 100 to change centimetres to metres: about 1,382 metres. That is about 1,380 metres.
maths.context: In Woven or Knitted you find that a knitted row holds far more thread than the cloth is wide. This problem follows that thread through a whole T-shirt front.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows something no one can see by looking: a small T-shirt holds more than a kilometre of thread.

maths.problem: In the Leaky Seam Test, a seam 8 cm long needs 8 stitches of 1 cm, or 16 stitches of half a centimetre. How many stitches a quarter of a centimetre long does it need? What is the pattern?
maths.answer: 32 stitches. Each time the stitch length is halved, the number of stitches doubles.
maths.explain: A quarter is half of a half. Halving the stitch length doubles the number of stitches: 8, then 16, then 32. The sewing time roughly doubles too.
maths.context: In the Leaky Seam Test you sew three seams of the same length with long, medium and short running stitches.
maths.why_maths: The pattern shows the cost of a tight seam: every halving of the gap doubles the work.

maths.problem: One family did the Leaky Seam Test. Their seam with 1 cm stitches let 12 seeds through. Their seam with half-centimetre stitches let 30 through. This is not the usual pattern. Name two things they should check.
maths.answer: They should check that both cloths were pulled equally flat over the tumbler, and that the second seam has no loose or missed stitch.
maths.explain: Shorter stitches should leave smaller gaps and let fewer seeds through. So something other than stitch length must have changed. A slack cloth opens less than a tight one. One loose stitch leaves one big gap. They could also check that each seam was rubbed 20 times.
maths.context: In the Leaky Seam Test you stretch seams over a tumbler, rub mustard seeds across them and count the seeds that fall through. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A number that breaks the pattern is a clue. Reasoning about it finds what went wrong in the test.

maths.problem: The Chindi Coaster has 10 warp threads and 16 rows of weft, so it has 160 crossings. A cotton sari has about 4,800 warp threads and about 22,000 rows of weft. About how many crossings hold the sari together?
maths.explain: Each row of weft crosses every warp thread once. So multiply: 4,800 times 22,000. 48 times 22 is 1,056. Then put back the five zeros: 105,600,000. That is 10 crore 56 lakh.
maths.context: In the Chindi Coaster project you weave a small mat on a card loom and count its crossings: the warp threads times the rows.
maths.why_maths: Counting crossings shows why a cloth with no glue and no knots still holds: friction acts at crores of places at once.

maths.problem: A male baya weaver is said to make up to 500 trips to build one nest, in about 18 days. About how many trips is that each day, at most? If he works 10 hours a day, about how often does he arrive with a new strip?
maths.answer: At most about 28 trips a day, so a new strip about every 21 minutes.
maths.explain: 500 divided by 18 is a little less than 28. Ten hours is 600 minutes. 600 divided by 28 is a little more than 21. So he would bring a new strip about every 21 minutes, all day, for 18 days.
maths.context: In the Chindi Coaster project you weave 16 rows in two short sittings. A male baya weaver weaves a whole nest with his beak.
maths.why_maths: Dividing turns two big numbers into something you can picture: one strip of grass every 21 minutes or so.

how_we_found_out.context: Cloth rots in the ground within years. So how do we know how long people have been weaving? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, archaeologists thought weaving began with farming, less than 10,000 years ago. The oldest cloth they had found was about that old, and settled villages seemed necessary for looms. The people of the Ice Age were pictured in animal skins. Cloth and string rot quickly, so nobody expected to find any. Then, in the 1990s, Olga Soffer and James Adovasio studied small lumps of fired clay from Pavlov and Dolní Věstonice, in today's Czech Republic. People had lived there about 26,000 years ago. Bohuslav Klíma had dug up the clay years earlier, and it had been stored as scraps. Under a lens, some lumps showed neat rows of crossing lines. Wet clay had once been pressed against woven cloth, nets and cord, and then baked in a fire. The cloth was gone, but the print stayed. Soffer and Adovasio counted several kinds of weave and knots for nets. So people were weaving about 15,000 years before farming. The work needed no village and no big loom, only skilled hands.
how_we_found_out.who: Olga Soffer and James Adovasio, archaeologists in the United States, and Bohuslav Klíma, a Czech archaeologist
how_we_found_out.when: The 1990s. Their first report on woven prints from Pavlov was published in 1996.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That weaving began with farming, less than 10,000 years ago, and that Ice Age people wore only skins. Prints of woven cloth in clay about 26,000 years old showed that weaving is far older.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman archaeologist looking through a lens at a small lump of brown fired clay, with an enlarged view beside it showing rows of crossing thread marks.

roots.context: We have learned how thread is woven, knitted and stitched into cloth, and how cloth is taken apart and used again. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Woven or Knitted, one loose end pulled out a whole row as a single thread. So a knitted sweater can go back to yarn and be knitted again. A woven cloth frays where it is cut, yet it can be cut and stitched into something new. The way a thing was made decides how it can be taken apart and made again.
deep_truth.habit: We call old cloth 'waste', as if a thing simply ends when we stop using it. We also sort things for reuse by their material alone. But two cloths of the same cotton have different second lives, because one was looped from a single thread and the other was crossed from many.
deep_truth.evidence: In Woven or Knitted, a row of the knitted piece came out as one long thread. In the Fray Test, the woven piece lost threads only at its cut edges and stayed whole inside. In The Sweater That Went Back to Wool, the cut pieces were wasted and the unravelled wool was not.

three.who_am_i: Your body is built from many tiny parts, held together in a particular arrangement. The food you eat is taken apart and built into you. So the material in you keeps changing, while you stay yourself.
three.what_is_life: Living beings were spinning and weaving long before people. A caterpillar spins, a baya weaves and a tailorbird stitches. Making is part of being alive.
three.what_is_this_world: In nature, almost nothing is thrown away for good. A cotton plant builds the fibre in cotton from air, water and sunlight. A shirt can become a quilt, then a duster, and at last soil that can grow new cotton.

roots.thread: A cotton plant builds fibre out of air, water and sunlight. People twist that fibre into one thread. From threads we make many kinds of cloth. They are woven, knitted, dyed and stitched in hundreds of ways across India. When a cloth wears out, its thread and fibre can become a quilt, a rug or new yarn. All these cloths are made of the same few things, which are fibre and thread, arranged in different ways. The fibre came from the same air and water that your own body is made from.

teachings.teaching: The philosopher Gargi Vachaknavi asks the sage Yajnavalkya a weaver's question. If all this world is woven, like warp and weft, on water, then on what is water woven? She asks again and again, down to the last thing on which everything is woven.
teachings.link: Gargi used the picture of a loom to ask what holds the world together. In this unit your child asks the same kind of question of a cloth, and finds threads, then plies, then fibres, then long molecules.

teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you see the cloud, the rain, the tree and the logger. Without any one of them, the paper would not be here.
teachings.link: The same is true of a cotton shirt. In it are the cotton plant, the soil and rain, the farmer, the spinner, the weaver or knitter, the dyer and the tailor.

science.text: The cellulose in every cotton fibre was built by a plant from carbon dioxide and water, using the energy of sunlight.
A whole, such as a cloth, can do things that none of its parts can do alone. Whether this means the whole is something more than its parts is still argued about by philosophers and scientists.

other_view.who: The Buddhist monk Nagasena, in the Milindapanha
other_view.view: Nagasena asks King Milinda whether the chariot is the wheels, the axle or the pole. It is none of them. 'Chariot' is only a name for the parts arranged together. In this view, 'cloth' and 'sweater' are also only names. There are threads arranged in a certain way, and no need to look for one last thing on which everything is woven.

practice.title: Follow one thread
practice.say: Hold the hem of your shirt up to the light. Find one thread and follow it slowly with your eyes. Watch it go over and under, or round its loops. Breathe slowly four times as you follow it. Now think of who touched this thread before you: a plant, a spinner, a weaver, a tailor.

playtest: The experiments, activities, games, project and challenges were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a city flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. Three things need old cloth that can be cut: a woven cotton cloth, a cotton T-shirt or banian, and a thin cotton cloth such as an old dupatta. In Woven or Knitted, check the T-shirt label for elastane first. Pulling one row of thread out of T-shirt cloth takes patience: try both cut edges, or use an old sock or sweater, whose yarn is thicker. In the Leaky Seam Test, the counts depend on how flat the cloth is pulled over the tumbler, so pull all three seams the same. In the Fray Test, a tightly woven cloth may hardly fray in 300 shakes: use the thinnest cloth you have, or shake longer. All sewing steps need a grown-up beside the child. The three videos have no address yet, so find and watch them before showing them.
